paragraphs.text: We now undertake to set out the life, character and deeds of holy Noah, and also, if we can, the loftiness of his mind. Philosophy itself has said that nothing is harder than to grasp the inner life of a human being; how much harder, then, to know the mind of a just man? Yet since the Lord God kept him back to renew the human race and to be a seedbed of justice, it is fitting that we too should describe him as a model for all to imitate, and that we should find rest in him from all the anxiety of this world, which we bear every day under its various upheavals. It shames me to outlive my sons; it wearies me. When we hear of so many misfortunes befalling those dearest to us, who is so strong that he can patiently bear to go on enjoying this light, and either to face in person or to take to heart the many waves and storms that beset the churches themselves? That is why we too had to seek this rest: so that, while we consider holy Noah with closer attention, we may also be refreshed, just as every kind of creature found rest in him from its labours and its sorrow.

This is also why he is called Noah, which in Latin means "just" or "rest." And indeed his parents said: "This one will give us rest from our labours, and from sorrow, and from the earth which the Lord God has cursed." If you think this refers to what actually happened, then, since the flood came in his time, it would seem that what was brought upon humanity was not rest but destruction, not relief from evils but a heaping up of miseries. But if you consider the mind of the just man, you will see that justice alone is born for others rather than for itself, and seeks not what is useful to itself but what is useful to all. It is justice that gives us rest from the works of iniquity; it is justice that calls us back from sorrow, because while we do what is just we fear nothing, in the security of a pure conscience, and we do not suffer grievous pain; for nothing causes greater pain than the guilt of sin. Let us also rest from every care of earthly life, which torments our body and soul with frequent pains and wears our life away.

Three sons were born to him: Shem, Ham and Japheth. These names signify "good," "evil" and "indifferent," so that he may be seen to have possessed goodness by the gift of nature, never to have been without the temptations of evil, and to have abounded in things indifferent, that is [?] as in a kind of equipment for the virtues. The reason why evil is placed in the middle is plain: the good of nature is present in everyone, and nature does not cast people into the light like shipwrecked sailors, but props them up with strength, so that they are not overwhelmed by the temptations of wickedness or give way as though powerless. It also protects and clothes them, as it were, with certain coverings of indifferent things, namely health, sound constitution, beauty, energy, wealth, glory and noble birth, so that, fortified with this dowry, they may guard the goodness of nature, hem in that evil so that it cannot do harm, and, having shut it in, strangle it. Do we not see here a kind of battle line of the virtues drawn up for combat, with the weaker troops in the middle and the stronger ones on the right and left, as on the wings, from which the whole line draws its strength?

Hence a certain Greek poet says: κακοὺς δ' εἰς μέσσον ἔλασσεν, that is, "but the bad he drove into the middle." In the same way, then, nature, like a good general acting at God's command, knowing that we are born for the battles of this world, has placed its goods in the first rank, the things that hinder in the second, and the things that help in the third, so that the enemy, shut in as it were in the middle, may be crushed by doubled forces wherever it turns, and may not wear down each of them in evenly matched fights or find a way to escape from the confines set by nature and spread more widely.

But since this is the order where they are born, whereas where they beget, Japheth is written first and Ham third, we must also explain the reason for that passage, so that no one may think we have said things contrary to what follows. The good, which resides as it were in a certain nobility of nature, comes first, while evil follows. For the mind's contrary thoughts certainly arise later. As long as these are, so to speak, shut up within and do not sprout like plants, they are held in the bosom of a good mind so that they do not come forth. For as long as evil remains in the will and not in entelechy, that is, in act and effect, the goodness of the governing mind, like a charioteer, holds back and reins in the wickedness that is trying to burst out. But when it has boiled up and broken out into an ulcer, then a just providence steps in, so that it cannot creep further and infect what lies near it, and so that the indifferent, which people commonly call a secondary good, does not give ground, as it might, being unable to resist an evil already boiling over. Therefore, so that the harmful poison may not spread more widely and, by breeding, infect very many with corruption, that first good, which is good by nature, changes its rank by changing its place, so as to bring help, as it were, to a struggling wing and to take over in the battle line the part that is under the greatest pressure. For a warrior's courage is needed in the more difficult positions, just as a good guard is present more often where the walls are weaker. And so that no part may be left without a defender, while that good supports the weaker parts, the indifferent takes the higher position, as though the more perfect good were assigning that part to it; for nothing is more perfect than virtue. Indifferent things do not have the strength of robust virtue, but they increase and spread its grace. This is why he was called Japheth, which in Latin means "breadth."

Not only did holy Noah abound in the begetting of sons; the whole human race also poured itself forth at that time more than ever. This does not seem to be without purpose. With the flood about to come, it ought not to be thought that the gift of fruitfulness was lacking to that generation which the flood swallowed up. Rather, the abundance of the human race is to be credited to divine grace, and the flood that followed is to be laid to the charge of our iniquities, since by our sins we turn away the Lord's mercy. So too in later times you will find that the coming barrenness of Egypt was preceded by as many years of fruitfulness. For it is the chief mark of virtue to begin with benefits and to sow grace beforehand. That is why David also says: "Of mercy and judgment I will sing to you, O Lord." The grace of kindness goes first; the reproof of sober discipline follows. It is God's doing, then, that good things are given first, and ours that they are changed.

God himself makes this plain when he says: "My spirit shall not remain in human beings, because they are flesh." The Holy Spirit is the spirit of wisdom, the spirit of knowledge. So he has wisdom, and he also has discipline, as Scripture says of Bezalel, who was commanded by divine oracle to make the sacred tabernacle, that he was filled with the spirit of understanding and discipline. This Spirit, then, is given to human beings, but does not remain. The reason it does not remain is stated: because they are flesh. For the nature of flesh resists discipline, since it obeys pleasure. And so it is written of the Lord Jesus alone: "He on whom you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit." For the Spirit remained in him whom no hindrances of fleshly corruption kept from holding to the rule of an uncorrupted and unmixed discipline, he whose flesh did not see corruption.

It is declared, then, that salvation would come to the nations through the one Lord Jesus, who alone could not have been just, when the whole race had gone astray, unless, being born of a virgin, he was by that privilege in no way bound by a guilty generation. "Behold," he says, "I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me"; so speaks the one who was thought just above all others. Whom, then, should I call just [?] except one free of these chains, one whom the chains of our common nature do not hold? All have been under sin since Adam; death reigned over all. Let the only just one come into the sight of God, of whom it is no longer said with a qualification, "He did not sin with his lips," but rather, "He committed no sin."

"Now there were giants on the earth in those days." The author of divine Scripture does not want these giants to be taken, as the poets take them, for sons of the earth. He says that they were begotten of angels and women, and he calls them by this name to convey the great size of their bodies. And let us consider whether men who devote themselves to the care of their flesh and take no care at all for the soul may not be like the giants, just as those who, in the poets' fable, sprang from the earth are said to have trusted in the bulk of their bodies and held the gods above in contempt. Or should we think them unlike? Though they are made of soul and body, they turn away from the strength of the mind, which is the most precious thing the soul has, and they show themselves imitators of this flesh, heirs, as it were, of their mother's dullness. So they labor in vain, laying claim to heaven with proud vows while they brood over earthly works. Because they have chosen the lower fellowship and despised the higher, they are guilty of sins committed by choice, and so they are condemned with greater severity.

Scripture often calls the angels sons of God, because souls are not begotten of any man. And so God did not disdain to call faithful men his sons. Just as men of upright life are called sons of God, so on the authority of the Scriptures we call those whose works are carnal sons of the flesh. For John the evangelist says that to as many as received the Lord Jesus, to those who believe in his name, he gave power to become sons of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. That is why you read afterward that the Lord was angry. He considered, that is, he knew, that man, set in the region of the earth and bearing flesh, could not be without sin, for the earth is a kind of place of temptations and the flesh an enticement to corruption. Even so, they had a mind capable of reason and the power of the soul poured into the body, yet they rushed headlong into a fall without any thought, and they refused to call themselves back from it. For God does not think as men do, so that some new opinion should occur to him, nor is he angry as though he could change. These things are written to show how bitter our sins are, which deserved to offend the Godhead. It is as though guilt had grown so great that even God, who by nature is moved by no anger, hatred or passion, seemed to be provoked to wrath.

He also threatened to destroy man. "From man to beast," he says, "and from the creeping things to the birds, I will destroy." What harm had the creatures without reason done? But they had been made for man's sake. Once the one for whose sake they were made was destroyed, it followed that they too should be destroyed, for there was no one left to use them. In a deeper sense, however, this shows that man is mind, which is capable of reason. For man is defined as a living, mortal, rational animal. So when the ruling part is extinguished, all sense is extinguished with it, because nothing is left for salvation once virtue, the foundation of salvation, has failed. Noah, however, is said to have found favor with God, to condemn the rest and to show the mercy of God. At the same time we are shown that the offenses of others do not cast a shadow on a just man, since he himself is kept as the seedbed of the whole race. He is praised not for noble birth but for the merit of justice and perfection. For the lineage of an upright man is a pedigree of virtues: as men are the offspring of men, so virtues are the offspring of souls. Families of men are ennobled by the splendor of their lineage, but the grace of souls is made glorious by the splendor of virtue.

"Now the earth was corrupted before God," he says, "and was filled with injustice." The cause of the earth's corruption is plain: the injustice of men had corrupted the earth. So the Lord God also says: "The time of every man has come before me, because the earth is filled with its iniquities." The time of all men is indeed in God's sight and in his will. This is not, as people commonly say, an appeal to a decree of fate. Still, I think it was said here with a special meaning. In his Gospel the Lord, about to redeem the human race by the passion of his body and to cleanse it with his blood and the sacrament of baptism, says: "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that the Son may also glorify you." In the flood the remnant of the human race was preserved through Noah's ark as a seedbed for the restoration and renewal to come, and that is why he said here first: "The time of every man has come, because the earth is filled with its iniquities." This was said in figure. In truth he says: "A remnant has been saved through the love of grace." And so the apostle cries out:

"Sin abounded, so that grace might abound all the more." "All flesh," he says, "had corrupted its way." Here he used "flesh" for earthly man, in whom the enticement of the flesh corrupted his way. If man had understood what gift he had received from God, he would surely not have allowed the flesh to stand in the way of the virtues of the soul. So the flesh was the cause of the soul's corruption as well. The flesh is a kind of region and dwelling place of pleasure. From it, as from a spring, rivers of desires and evil passions burst forth and flood far and wide. In them the soul's oarsmen are swamped once the helmsman has been thrown overboard, when the mind itself is overcome as if by storms and gales and gives up its place. He says well that man corrupted the way of his own nature. For his way lay in paradise, on that path of blessedness, in that flower of the virtues, in that incorruptible grace, and he defiled this way with earthly footprints. Other versions read "his way," that is, God's way. Scripture usually expresses this with the words "of the Lord."

But now I think we should speak of Noah's ark itself. Anyone who studies it closely will find the figure of the human body drawn in its construction. What does God mean when he says, "Make yourself an ark of squared timbers"? We call "square" whatever is well balanced in all its parts and consistent with itself. So these words affirm that God is the author of our body and the maker of our nature, and they show that the work itself is perfect. It is plain that the limbs of man are square. Look at a man's chest, look at his belly: each is equal in length and breadth, unless the natural measure is exceeded when the belly is swollen with pleasures and feasting. As for the feet and hands, the arms, thighs and legs, which are fourfold, who does not see this at a glance? Many of them, though not of the same length or breadth, still keep a certain proportion, so that in them too a fitting measure and ratio come together: the length, as he says, greater than the breadth, and the breadth greater than the height. The timber of the ark has three dimensions, since he ordered a length of three hundred cubits, a breadth of fifty cubits and a height of thirty cubits. In the same way our body has a greatest, a middle and a least dimension: the greatest in length, the middle in breadth, the least in height. Yet the whole body, woven together from its separate limbs, looks square. In common speech too we call people "square" when we judge them to be not outsized in height but strong and sturdy in build.

Nor should we pass over in silence what he means by "You shall make nests in the ark." I think this was said with reference to nature, because our whole body is woven together like a nest. So the vital spirit can reach every part of the inner organs and flow out from our ruling part through each of the limbs. Our eyes are nests of a sort, and sight settles into them. The hollows of our ears are nests, through which hearing pours in and drops down as into a deep pit. The nostrils are a nest that draws scent to itself. A fourth nest, larger than the rest, is the opening of the mouth. In it taste is nourished until it grows full, and from it the voice flies out. In it lies the tongue, which, like an instrument of the voice, shapes its sounds with skilled sweetness, and though it has no reason itself, utters a voice that has reason. The skull is a nest, and so is that membrane which keeps the brain warm and holds it within itself. The lungs and heart are nests. The lungs are the nest of our breath, the breath we draw and by which we are sustained in this life. The heart is the nest of blood and of spirit. For it has two chambers. With one it receives the blood as into a pocket and passes it on into the veins. With the other, supplied from the first, it conducts it into the arteries in a continuous flow. The stronger bones also have nests, for they are hollow inside, and the marrow lies in these cavities. In the softer inner organs themselves are the nests of desire or of pain. Anyone who considers other parts will find still more nests in this structure of the human body. That is why I think the psalmist spoke not only mystically but also with reference to nature when he said: "For the sparrow has found itself a home, and the turtledove a nest for herself, where she may lay her young." For now in this body there is a nest of modesty, where once there was a nest of irrational desire. Where lust once nourished misshapen offspring, now the inheritance of lovely chastity grows up.

"You shall coat it with pitch," he says. The human body is made of many bones and sinews and other parts. So it holds together both outside and inside, joined in a fitting framework, and it is kept together by its own condition, which the Greeks call hexis [?]. In this way the spirit poured in and shut inside, or the spiritual substance at work within, is bound as if by twin bonds. It does not wander off but is held in a fitting and harmonious unity and a strong connection. That is why the ark is ordered to be sealed with pitch, for pitch is by nature powerfully binding. So in Greek it is called asphaltos, from asphaleia, that is, "security," because it joins what is separate and binds it with an unbreakable bond, so that you would think the parts held together by a natural unity. For this reason the ark is sealed with pitch inside and out, so that the joint may not easily break.

Elsewhere, in Exodus, that ark which stands in the holy place, an image that imitates the intelligible world, is also gilded inside and out. As gold is more precious than pitch, so the ark in the holy place is more excellent than this one. Here he simply wrote "timbers." There he did write "timbers," but he specified timbers that do not rot, thus declaring the merits of the saints. He also added there that the carrying poles were immovable, because the position of the saints is stable and firm: under the guidance of virtue they have followed the path of an upright life and turned away from the company of corruption. This ark, however, being in the flood, was driven this way and that in uncertain motion. For the state of sinners is unstable, and their life, exposed to corruption by what is like a flood of overflowing passions, wanders in fickle error.

Nor should we pass over the fact that, after saying "And you shall make the ark three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide and thirty cubits high," he added: "Drawing it together you shall make the ark, and you shall finish it to a cubit at the top." In this way he joined the head of man, like a royal citadel, to the rest of the body, which was squared gracefully in its fitting measure. From the head all the senses would be distributed to the other parts of the body, and above all the eyes, posted by nature's foresight as lookouts and guardians, would survey from above almost the whole state of our city. The mind itself is located there, according to the opinion of most, and especially of Solomon, who says: "The eyes of the wise man are in his head." There, as in an imperial court, it gathers to itself a council of the virtues. Surrounded by this retinue it is itself more secure, and from a kind of inner sanctuary it imparts government to the whole body that it watches over [?], and knows how to give answers. Through these we can not only look back at ourselves, and not only see what lies before our feet, but also gaze on the secrets of heaven itself with the deep insight of wisdom. There, then, lies the whole sum of our safety, and there our grace. From there the whole body gains protection and beauty as well, a beauty that blossoms first in the face. For it is fitting that the splendor of the royal court should surpass the rest, since there, as the use is greater, so is the splendor.

Look at each of the parts of the human form that seem designed for some use: the eyes for seeing, the ears for hearing, the nostrils for smelling, the mouth for speaking. They serve their uses in such a way that they also give beauty. How disfigured the faces of the blind are! And what wonder if a human face without eyes is disfigured, when heaven itself has no beauty without the sun? Without the sun our days are gloomy, and nights without the moon give no pleasure, for these are, as it were, the eyes of the world. Take away the light of the stars, and even heaven has a kind of disfigurement of blindness. Consider the lashes that border the orb of the eyes and are stretched in front of them like a battle line, so that the pupil may not be harmed by dirt or a cloud of dust, and which catch anything blown in that could harm the eye. How unsightly it is if they fall out through inflammation, if the eyelid shrinks, or if the eyebrows are shaved off, which shine like precious necklaces set with gems!

The ears too are as comely in appearance as they are necessary in use, and anyone who cuts them off disfigures the whole face. In them nature has worked out her design so carefully that the very windings of their hollows, curved with wonderful foresight, are of great benefit: sound does not suddenly strike the inner recesses of the head. Indeed we often see many people startled by an unexpected blare, and stunned and frightened by the sound of a voice or an uproar. The wax itself that forms within these windings binds the hearing as with a kind of glue. At the same time, if some sound strikes too violently, it is broken and slowed, so that, announced in advance, it soothes rather than shaking the inner parts by surprise. And if little worms try to get into the ear, they are caught in the wax as if in birdlime.
Snub noses seem contrary to nature. And if the nostrils are cut off, how can life go on once the passage for breathing is gone? How much more such a face is thought to be a beast's than a man's!

How pleasing is the covering with which the hair clothes the head, like the bodyguards of a royal palace, so that the wind may not harm the brain, nor the rain beat on it, nor the sun scorch it! Yet nature so restores the hair that it pleases either long or cut short according to sex, according to age, and often according to the season and time of year. In old men gray hair is pleasing; in boys it is a portent. In summer we like to be cropped close, in winter to let it grow more freely. Long hair is an ornament to women and a disgrace to men. Indeed the apostle said this more plainly: "Does not nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair it is a dishonor to him, but if a woman has long hair it is her glory?"

What shall I say of the royal gateway itself, through which the speeches of the court come forth, revealers of our mind and messengers of the soul? What of the very row of teeth, which by their work both supply strength to the whole body and also shape the voice itself?

If any one of them falls out, the voice limps. We have spoken at some length about the head, because all the senses had to be placed at the top, so that from there all the duties might be shared out among the other parts. Next to our head at the back is the neck, and to the right and left are the arms, which guard the imperial citadel like a faithful garrison. In short, the parts of us nearer the head are the stronger, and these are the more excellent. The chest too is a kind of sanctuary of wisdom. The stomach, as physicians say, is a kind of witness and confidant of the head's secrets and shares in its feelings, and the head passes on to it all its states, whether healthy or ill. The sides, buttocks, thighs and legs show by their very appearance the breadth of the measure, and so do the steps of the feet, which, though they look rather narrow, become broader when we walk.

He also added well: "You shall make the door on the side." By this he indicated the part of the body through which we usually discharge the waste of our food, so that he might surround with more abundant honor those parts of the body we think less noble. Scripture expressed this much more gracefully than what Socrates is said to have spoken in Plato's book. Either Socrates himself or Plato, who was in Egypt, could have read this in the writings of Moses or learned it from those who had read them. Moved by the seemliness of the discovery, he thought a door had been opened for him to proclaim the design of our maker. He praised him because it was especially fitting to decency that he turned certain ducts and outlets of our channels away to the back, so that our sight would not be offended when the bowels are purged. But the apostle says: "The members of the body that seem weaker are necessary," surpassing the descriptions of philosophy with one simple word, "and those members of the body that we think less noble we surround with more abundant honor, and our unseemly parts have more abundant seemliness." For it is there above all that the sign of our sobriety and temperance is recognized. Gluttons are either swollen with indigestion to the point of danger or else often have their bowels loosened and emptied out.

The apostle also applied this well to the members of the Church. For what are our unseemly and superfluous parts, if not luxury and wantonness? Suppose someone was entangled in them in the time of his youth and then, having reached a more mature age, comes to baptism. He renounces the past, strips off his former habits, lays down his sins, is buried with the Lord Jesus, and the world is crucified to him and he to the world. Once he has been granted the remission of sins, does he not have more abundant seemliness than the catechumen whose life was thought more innocent? To use the example of the apostle himself: he was a Jew, he was a persecutor. Called to the grace of Christ, he became an apostle. And because more had been forgiven him, he began to love more and to labor more abundantly than all the apostles. He was made a chosen vessel and sent as teacher of the Gentiles. Did he not obtain a richer and more honorable

glory than most of the apostles themselves, though before he had been without honor and without glory, when he persecuted the Church of God? That poor man, that cripple in the church, has himself redeemed you by his prayers. And to disclose greater mysteries: what is so lowly as the Gentile people? It was poor, since it had none of the oracles of God. It was weak and lame in both feet, since it had believed neither the law nor the gospel. Yet when it was called it believed, and when it was baptized it received grace. And so, because more was forgiven it, it loves more. The Jewish people stayed behind, lame in only one foot, though it limps even in the law itself. So the people that was held most glorious lost everything: the wonderful counselor, the skilled master builder and the wise listener. This people, which was lowly, gained everything by the title of faith and the trophy of the martyrs, and it glories in the fellowship of the angels. Plato, then, applied whatever brilliance of speech he could, but the apostle, who had the Spirit of God, revealed the mystery. Enough has been said about the door, since those who were behind have become first.

Now let us ask what the Lord meant when he said: "You shall make the lower parts of the ark with two chambers and three chambers." From the words "lower parts" we see that he wanted us to understand, aptly, that the receptacles of food should be placed low down, that is, the organs that digest the food they receive. For food is corruptible, and what is corruptible is to be compared not with higher things but with lower ones. Food is also carried downward. A small portion of it serves the strength and nourishment of the body, and the rest is carried down to be purged through the bowel. Because the intestines, through

which the waste of food passes down, exist for this, our maker so arranged them that they do not run straight from the stomach to the bottom but are coiled and folded back, so that our life might be prolonged. If a man's intestines, which receive the food and carry it down, were straight, it would pass straight through without any delay. We would have to be hungry all the time and feasting all the time, or else collapse at once when the supply of nourishment ran out. As it is, the food lingers in the twofold and threefold folds and windings of the intestines. Moving down little by little, it supplies strength, pours its juice into the body, keeps us satisfied and puts off the desire to eat. There is no sudden outpouring or abrupt emptying, no appetite that cannot be filled, no insatiable lust for feasting. Otherwise there would first be want and hunger, and then from these would follow eating without pause. And what is more unsightly than always to be devoted to the belly, which must be emptied when it is filled and filled when it is emptied? What third thing remains but death, mixed in among the very food and feasts? How could people prolong their lives any further if they were eating and hungry at once, drinking and thirsty at once, emptying out everything they had taken before they were even full, and hungry again at once? As it is, while the food moves down little by little, the providence of nature moderates both hunger and indigestion. First the food is worked over in the stomach, which many call the upper belly. Then it is cooked in the liver and digested by its heat. Its juice is shared out to certain parts of the inner organs, and from it the whole body gains strength, as the growth of the young and the endurance of the old amply testify. The rest of the food flows down into the belly, which we all call simply the belly and many call the lower belly. From there the dung, which has come down already full of corruption, must be discharged through that door on the side.

Natural design has arranged all this with great skill at God's command. Yet unless we keep a measure in eating and in our conduct, a flood rises as if from overflowing passions, and a kind of ruin falls on the whole body. Excess kindles lust, produces indigestion and causes corruption. So the bowels are either stretched by an inner hardness and racked with pains, or else, through the undigested moisture of food and the harshness of indigestion, a certain inner lining of the intestines is scraped. For their lining is said to be double, like a sheet of papyrus. The outer layer, which the experts, or those who have looked into the matter more carefully, call continuous, runs straight from top to bottom. The inner layer is woven on, as it were, at the sides, and so they say that it does not come apart entirely when it is scraped; if the inner layer were continuous, a tear in it could not be healed. They say that the remains of food cling there because they are held up at the joinings, and that if these joinings come apart, half-digested food and drink pass straight through.

This is the flood of man. So it seems to me that through the figure of this ark God wished to teach us how to be safe from this particular flood. Corruption is the cause of the flood. Where it has crept in, the waters are opened and all the fountains of desire boil up, so that the whole body is drowned in so great and deep a torrent of vices. Nothing subjects a man to so wretched a slavery as lust and desires of that kind, which press down the wretched conscience under a heavy yoke of crimes, so that it cannot raise itself, since it has lost the freedom of innocence. The greatest remedy against this flood, then, is to put the righteous man first and to choose him to carry out the heavenly command. Who is the righteous man in us but the vigor of the mind, which shuts up within this ark every kind of living creature that is on the earth? So you too must restrain all your irrational passions, subject all your senses to the mind, and accustom them to the commands of the soul. Do not let your desires fly out, or your lust go out into the crowd. Then through the rational mind you will be able to free even your irrational and unclean sins from all danger of the flood.

"Everything that is on the earth," he says, "shall die." But what wrong had the dumb animals done? Why were they subjected to punishment when they have no sense of sin? In war, when a general is killed by the enemy, his army dies with him and all its military strength is broken. In the same way it did not seem at odds with justice that when man perished, the cattle and all the irrational animals should die with him. For the Lord God had given man a kind of royal power over every kind of living creature, so that he might rule over all the birds, wild beasts and animals with the authority of a ruler. Indeed, whenever pestilence comes because the air has been corrupted, the dread plague first infects the irrational creatures, and above all it strikes dogs, horses, oxen and those animals that are seen to live among men; and then the force of the disease takes hold of the human race as well.

This, then, is the first reason why the statement is just, as I think. The second is that no one blames nature because the other members of our body die when the head alone is taken away, although we see many people survive after their hands and feet have been cut off. The other members do not have the same privilege as the head. So when the head is cut off, from which our senses go out into the rest of the body, all the members die with it, and yet no one finds the Maker's providence lacking in this, or faults the frailty of human nature. Likewise, then, let no one now object: man is the head and a kind of chief of the other animals, and when he dies, it should not seem strange if the other living creatures die with him.

The third reason is that the animals lacking reason were created not for their own sake but for man's. They were commanded to exist for man's sake, so that the human condition might stand above them by their subjection. Indeed the prophet attributes them to man's favor when he says: "You have put all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, and the beasts of the field as well, the birds of the air and the fish of the sea." For all those things exist for his sake, some for usefulness, some for delight, some for pleasure. It followed, then, that when man, for whose sake they were made, was wiped from the face of the earth, they too should be wiped out in the same destruction. This is the explanation according to the simple reading.

A higher and deeper interpretation adds this. When the soul is bowed down under the heavy weight of the passions and is drowned, as it were, in the surge of various desires, all earthly thoughts and lusts rush headlong; for the more serious the crimes each sinner commits, the more insolent he becomes. Wickedness grows by habit and practice, and boldness is nourished by impunity. So he withdraws from all regard for what is honorable, and everything earthly in him dies through the bitterness of deadly sin, which destroys the sinner with a true and everlasting death; no one dies a heavier death than the one who lives in sin. The individual passions die in him. Sight dies, which reports sin, which fixes itself on a deceitful woman, which is captured by the beauty of another's face, which the eyes of a harlot have bound and the look of a prostitute has ensnared. Does not a man seem to die who has driven the dart of lust into himself, who has rushed of his own accord into the pit of death? Hearing dies too, when it carries crimes back, when it reports the words of an adulterer who tempts, when it plants in the mind the words of the harlot who seduces a young man with much flattering speech and binds him with the snares of her lips. The voice dies by silence, if it does not confess to God. It dies by much talking, for it is written for you: "In much speaking you will not escape sin." It dies through anger, when it goes beyond the measure of retribution.

In short, every sense dies if it serves iniquity. And so, since everything earthly dies in the flood and only the righteous man remains forever, it is said to him: "I will establish my covenant with you." For he is the heir of divine grace, the possessor of the heavenly inheritance, the sharer of the most blessed honors. When men die, they usually pass on their estate by a will, and the inheritance does not pass while the testator is alive. But God, since he is eternal, pours out on the righteous the inheritance of his divine being; and he, who lacks nothing, gives what is his without any loss through the giving, and is not burdened by those who share his honors. He rather takes greater joy in what we enjoy. Indeed the Lord Jesus, though he was rich, became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich. He sealed both testaments with his blood, to make us coheirs of his life and heirs of his death, so that we might have both a share in his life and the benefit of his death. He grants much to the righteous man when he says, "I will establish my covenant with you," because the rational and faithful man is himself God's covenant. He himself is God's inheritance and possession. In him is the power of the divine testament, in him the fruit of judgment, in him the inheritance of the promise. Of him David said: "Behold, sons are the inheritance of the Lord, the fruit of the womb is his reward." But now, keeping to the explanation of the deeper mystery, let us go on to the rest.

"Go into the ark," he says, "you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous in this generation." Clearly this passage too confirms the truth of the prophetic saying that the fool is a fool for himself alone, while the wise man is wise for himself and for many. So because of Noah the righteous, his household too is saved in the flood. Likewise those sailing at sea, and an army in war, are kept safe from danger by another's help, if the sailors do not lack a skilled pilot and the army does not lack a prudent general. But because a good general has a good army, we also see that the righteous man's praise is not passed over here: he so trained his household that it shone by sharing in his virtue, and his kin deservedly found salvation. Nor is it an objection that afterwards either his son or his wife did wrong. The righteous man was asleep when his son went astray. As for the woman, being of the weaker sex and shaken by the weight of the danger, believing that the whole world was perishing in a divine fire, why are you surprised if she could not follow her husband, when the righteous man himself, though warned by angels, barely escaped? And what wonder is it if error creeps up on a man, or his vigilance slackens? Find fault, then, because the righteous man also got drunk!

But I think these matters should be kept for their proper place. Now let us consider what remains. He spoke well when he said, "for I have seen that you are righteous in this generation." Many seem righteous to men, few to God. Men judge one way, God another: men by outward appearance of life, God by purity of mind and the truth of virtue. Men approve what is outside; God examines what is within. He added "in this generation" with careful thought, so as neither to condemn those before nor to exclude those after, and to show that the flood was rightly brought about for the destruction of that generation, which had no share in justice.

So much for the literal sense. But a higher sense invites us to think that the vigor of the mind is in the soul, and the soul in the body, what the father of a household is in his house. What the mind is in the soul, the soul is in the body. If the mind is safe, the house is safe, the soul is safe; if the soul is unharmed, the flesh is unharmed. A sober mind restrains all the passions, governs the senses, and rules speech. That is why the Lord says well to the righteous man, "Go in," that is, go into yourself, into your mind, into the ruling part of your soul. There is safety, there is the helm; outside is the flood, outside is danger. But if you are within, you are safe outside too, for where the mind is master of itself, the thoughts are good and the deeds are good. If no vice overshadows the mind, the thoughts are sincere. If chastity is your concern and temperance is dear to your heart, no flame of lust blazes up and no sores of sickness spread; for sobriety of mind is the medicine of the body.

Now let us consider why he orders that clean animals be brought into the ark seven by seven, male and female, but unclean ones two by two, so that seed might be preserved for the whole earth. In my opinion, he declares that a clean seven goes in, because the number seven is clean and holy: it is mixed with no other number and is not generated by another. So it is called a virgin, because it generates nothing from itself. Rightly, then, as having no part in childbirth and free of union with a woman, the seven, though it is called by a feminine noun, has the grace of a male sanctification. For "every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord," that is, holy. And in the prophet you have: "She escaped and gave birth to a male," that is, a holy one. The number two, however, is not full, because it is divided, and what is not full is considered empty. But the number seven is full, because the seven is like the ten, and like that first number, for the alpha bears the likeness of him who always is, from whom flow and are set in motion the powers in every kind of thing. So much for the natural sense.

To speak now of the moral sense: there is no doubt that the irrational part of our soul is divided into the five senses, the voice and the generative faculty, and these seem feminine by nature, because our senses quickly creep toward material and worldly things. Hence it is clear that their substance is of a softer nature. But to a learned and diligent man all things are clean, because the wisdom and virtue of a trained man pour into them a manly firmness. So by the judgment of the prudent man and the purpose of the one who governs them, they are transferred from the quality of the weaker sex into a stronger substance. For the wise man's judgment is solid and fixed, not changeable like that of the unwise and foolish man, who wavers in uncertain counsel, or of the wicked man, who chooses not what is true and just but what is convenient or useful to himself, and so separates himself from the truth and sets himself apart from justice. Justice is a single good, regarded for its own sake and valued only for its own worth; but iniquity, divided as it were, [?] is bent now by hatred, now by gain, and confuses what ought to be kept distinct. For the fool changes like the moon. Disfigured by the varying mixture of humors that change his color, he stains his soul with foul contagion until it looks like a leper's body, often mingling wholesome thoughts with harmful ones.

But perhaps, since you see that clean and unclean animals are ordered to be brought into the ark, you may rightly be troubled, because I said that unseemly debates should not be mixed with honorable ones. I do not deny that there are in our soul certain seeds and, as it were, beginnings of irrational movements, some clean and some not clean. For human nature is capable of opposites, so that both wickedness and virtue can enter it. Rightly, then, at the beginning of this book, which is Genesis, you read of the knowledge of good and evil in the figure of a tree in the middle of paradise. Of this tree of the knowledge of good and evil it was commanded that it must not be tasted, because our mind, in which knowledge and learning reside, takes in the notion of good and evil. So the Maker of nature, just as he kept back animals to propagate or restore their kind, so that the whole earth might be filled again with the seed of living creatures, likewise did not think that the earthly substance of our body should be left empty of passions of this sort, which are like unclean animals. When that substance is gorged with delights and luxury, as if by a flood, it is tossed about by these passions. But when a man has drained off by sobriety and self-control the flood of overflowing passions and has uncovered a kind of dry ground in the soul, he begins to bring life to his body and purity to the soul, whose guide is wisdom.

It is also worth asking why the flood came seven days after Noah entered the ark and brought in the animals. It does not seem idle that neither more nor fewer days intervened, but just as many as there were at the founding of the world. For the world was made in six days, and on the seventh day God rested from his works. By this sign he showed that he himself is the author both of the world and of the flood. He founded the world because of his goodness; he brought the flood because of what our sins deserved. So men were reminded, even by the number of days in which the world was founded, that they ought to reconcile their Creator not only with tears and prayer but with the amendment of their lives. The Lord, then, gave time for repentance, wishing rather to pardon than to punish, so that he might drive them, held in suspense by the terror of the coming flood, to ask for pardon; and so, while they shuddered at the danger of approaching death, they might renounce ungodliness and injustice. The second point is that from this too we may gather the mercy of the Lord, who is merciful beyond measure: he was willing to forgive in a few days, if they had repented, an offense of many years, drawn out from the founding of the world right to its end. For God forgets sin and rewards virtue, as he himself says in the prophet: "I am, I am he who blots out iniquities, and I will not remember them. But you, remember, and let us go to judgment; declare your iniquities, that you may be justified." For when he sees that true virtue has been restored to the soul, he grants it such honor that he not only pardons its former sins but also bestows grace and justification. So he waited until the seventh day, the very day on which he rested from his work, so that if pardon were sought and amendment followed, he too might rest from his anger.

We have also taken care not to pass over the fact that he said the flood lasted forty days and added "forty nights." We know that "day" is the name for the time marked by the sun as it lights the earth, and "night" for the time the surrounding darkness separates from the brightness of day. Often we use "day" so as not to include the night, and often so as to include it; for when we speak of a month of thirty days, we mean the nights as well. So, since it would have been enough for Moses to say that the flood lasted forty days, the question is why he added "and forty nights." Some who came before us understood it this way: that it was meant to show the destruction of both men and women in the flood. They referred the day to the man, as purer and like the light, and the night to the woman, who is described as created while the man was asleep. Further, the man comes first, as the originator who rouses the woman's power and stirs her to childbearing; he is more conspicuous through public activity, while she is more hidden, as if shut up within the walls of the house and close to the night. She came into being second, was formed from the man's rib, and owes the grace of her creation to the one above her; she is also subject to the privilege of the superior number, and by her practice of giving birth she is to be compared with material things. But the number of the danger matches in both, because their sins also matched; rightly, then, the lengths of time do not differ, because the guilt of their offenses did not differ.

Many also inquire with no small care why the flood lasted forty days. We can say that the material number is assigned to sadder things, that is, to the destruction of creation, while the seven is assigned to the founding of the whole world, that is, to happier things. But perhaps it matters that the law too was given over forty days. For that many days Moses kept watch and stayed on Mount Sinai while he received the commandments of the law. Rightly, then, the precepts for avoiding sin are given in the same number in which the penalty for guilt was paid, so that we may learn that in the same span of life in which guilt deserving punishment can be committed, praise ought to be won by amendment. So now forty days are prescribed no longer for punishment but for life, so that in this number, by fasting and more frequent prayer, we may lighten the punishments of our sins and, intent on the commandments of the law, correct our error by devotion and faith. And so, through the Lord's resurrection, the fortieth day is no longer reckoned the last but the first, and from it life is counted, where before the number of death was reckoned toward the end of the world and the destruction of the human race.

"And I will blot out," he says, "every resurrection of flesh from the face of the earth." O the beauty of heavenly words, if one examines them with the fitting understanding of a devout mind! God is angered at our sins, yet he does not forget his compassion. He threatens punishment, yet he did not allow utter destruction. He tempers vengeance and holds back severity. He says he will blot out flesh not from the earth but from the face of the earth. He shakes off the blossom but keeps the roots. He allows the strength of human nature to remain in the depths, so that what suffers on the surface may persist unharmed within and, free from harm, be kept to replace those who are not liable to guilt. He was right to say "I will blot out," as one blots out letters, which are erased without damaging the books or diminishing the tablets. The ink is erased, but the wood remains. Letters are erased, often so that better ones may be written; the ink is removed, but the substance is not destroyed. "I will blot out," he says, "the corruption of the flesh, so that I may write incorruption. I will blot out the resurrection of flesh from the face of the earth, so that I may write those who rise in heaven. I will blot out from the book of the earth, so that I may write in the book of life." Let them be blotted out, my Lord, O Lord, let the letters of iron be blotted out quickly, so that the letters of Christ may be written. Let the earthly resurrection be abolished, so that heavenly grace may overflow. Come, Moses, make ready your lap, receive the law, take up the letters, which divine mercy will no longer blot out. Take up the tablets, which the Lord will establish forever. If only you yourself do not break them! My own guilt would have taken them from me as well, had the Lord not given them back. You were indeed rightly angry, Moses, that those who did not offer obedience should not have God's privileges. But I think that you broke them not for me but for the Jews. You broke them for the Jews; you received them back for me. The first were broken so that the later ones might remain. You broke them in the hearts of the Jews; for what use was it for them to hold tablets whose commandments they could not keep? See, they say they hold the second tablets, but they do not hold them. They say they read the divine letters, but they do not read them. Moses says that the tablets were written by the finger of God. They do not read the finger of God; they read iron. They see the ink; they do not see the Spirit of God. But the Church does not know ink; it knows the Spirit. That is why Paul knew how to write not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. O sacrilegious and foolish Jewish people! A man writes by the Spirit of God, and a man brought up under the law at that, and they want God to have written with ink and not with the Spirit.

So, to return to what we were saying: God blots out the rising-up of flesh as one blots out written letters. This shows that he blotted out the excess of human birth because of its impiety, as one erases the shapes of letters, but preserved the substance and the life of the human race, like the lasting tablets, so that a remnant seed might sprout from it. That statement also seems to agree with this meaning where he says: I will blot out, he says, every rising-up of flesh. In the ordinary course of nature, cleansing seems to be the opposite of rising up, since cleansing cuts back and checks the overgrowth of what rises. Yet everything that is cleansed loses its outward form but keeps its substance and improves it. So by the cleansing of the flood the Lord checked the bodily habits and way of life of that generation, which had fallen away from the beauty of nature and the loveliness of the gift it had received. So much for the literal sense. As for the higher sense, the image of the flood is a type of the cleansing of our soul. So when our mind [?] has washed itself clean of the allurements of this world in which it once delighted, it wipes away the filth of its old desire with good thoughts, as if it were soaking up the bitterness of streams that were once muddy with purer waters.

And Noah did, it says, everything that the Lord God commanded him. The righteous man receives commandments; the slave receives orders. The one who carries out whatever he has undertaken to do is counted as a friend, while the one who wavers in obedience is consigned to the burden of slavery. Indeed the Lord Jesus also says in the Gospel: You are my friends if you do what I command you. I will no longer call you servants. So Noah is commanded as a friend, as one who would carry out what was commanded with strong love and sober judgment. Nor was the Lord mistaken in his judgment. The righteous man fulfilled everything: not a part, but everything that was commanded him, and so he receives the testimony of divine Scripture. And do not think it superfluous that the text puts "Lord" and "God" together (for God is in the Lord and the Lord is in God). It does so that you may understand the command as shared by the Father and the Son. Some before us, however, have interpreted it like this: by saying "Lord" and "God" in this place, Scripture expressed the twofold power of one who was going to punish and one who was going to pardon. Because here he first punishes sinners, it said "Lord" first, and because afterwards he grants that the seed of the righteous man be propagated, it named "God" afterwards. Indeed, when he is about to make the world, he is called God: In the beginning God made heaven and earth. And God said: Let there be light.

There is also a point here that deserves more than a passing glance: the flood comes in Noah's six hundredth year, <in the seventh month,> on the twenty-seventh day of the month. No one doubts that the seventh month falls in springtime, when growing things increase, the field is in labor, and the earth and the living creatures alike pour forth their young. So he sent the flood at the moment when those punished in the midst of their abundance would grieve the more. Then vengeance was more terrible, as though God were saying: "See, rich nature has brought forth everything by the grace of the generous providence of God; the earth, made more fruitful, has made everything sprout for man's use. Fields of wheat are on view, the plains are filled with barley, the leaves of the trees are clothed with the blossoms of fruit to come. The earth does not fail in its service, nor do the beasts fail in their duties, which they discharge in their regular births, so that man may lack nothing. Man alone fails in his part. He does not know his author, by whom everything is supplied to him; he neglects his creator. Man despises the one who rewards him, though God did not despise his own work. Let everything perish along with man, for whose sake everything was born. Let man be consumed in his riches; let him die with his dowry." The earth had done no wrong before man and had erred in none of its fruits; it knows that it has degenerated in man alone, bearing thorns and thistles instead of fruits. The one gift that was truly admirable, the ruling part of the mind, has perished. Why then are all those things kept? The reason the water is not poured in after the harvest is gathered is so that the earth would not feel it as a benefit rather than a flood. Indeed, among the Egyptians the Nile overflows in springtime, though in a different month, so that the earth may soften for sowing and receive the seeds cast into it in a gentler bosom and a kindlier lap. The fact that the flood comes in Noah's six hundredth year seems to point to Adam's creation on the sixth day. The same number, the one called even, is kept both in the author of the race and in its restorer, since the number six is the source of sixty and of six hundred. The same month, moreover, is called both the first and the seventh. But we ought rather to note first that after the flood, in springtime, the work of cultivating the fields is restored and the calm, fertile soil begins to bring forth its produce. This signifies that God would never have brought about the destruction of men by the same number and at the same season with which he made the beginning, had he not been offended by monstrous crimes. At the same time the reckoning of the season and the number promises pardon, because even in his anger he is reminded by such earlier grounds of his own benefits not to wipe out entirely the substance of those whom he himself had given.

And all the fountains of the deep burst forth, and the floodgates of heaven were opened. Scripture has fittingly expressed the force of the flood by saying that heaven and earth were stirred up together, the elements from which the whole beginning of this world is made. So the human race, hemmed in, is pressed hard by masses of water flooding in from every side. So much for the literal sense. As for the higher sense, heaven is a symbol of the human mind, while the name "earth" signifies the body and the senses. Great, then, are the shipwrecks when the whirlwind and storm of the mind, the body and all the senses are mingled together. Let us weigh the words carefully. Often the deceit and guile of the mind spread their poison, yet the sobriety and continence of the body cover over the mind's wickedness. The mind is often unsteady, uncertain in its faith and its opinions, yet the flesh keeps free of pleasures and luxury, so that frugality excuses the mind's error. This is the case with many heretics, who make a show of bodily continence so as to win credit for their teaching by the testimony of sober flesh. Though they are unsteady in understanding, they are thought somewhat more excusable because they are less shameful. But at times the poisons of the mind and the contagion of bodily obscenity confound all sense and vigor. The spirit, unsteady in its uncertain movement, reeking with the ink of malice, inflamed with the fury of cruelty, is spurred on to bodily vices as well. The avaricious disposition, impatient of modest means, is driven headlong by the craving for luxury and the lust to squander into the crime of seeking another's life. Then the flood is great, with all the passions assailing at once. Then folly, injustice, rashness, wickedness and treachery seem to pour out from the upper part, as from the floodgates of the mind. Then from the fountain of the earthly body burst forth lust, drunkenness and luxury, and finally the downfalls of every kind of crime, which utterly sap both the strength of the body and the vigor of the mind.

And God shut the ark from outside. The meaning according to the letter is plain. The ark had to be shut and secured with a safe defense, so that the roaming streams of the flood could not get into it. An interpretation in a higher sense is also fitting, if we take the human body, which this ark described here prefigures, as enclosed in skin and protected from cold and heat. God the craftsman clothed it in a natural covering to protect all its limbs and dressed it in a kind of wrapping spread around it, so that it would neither freeze with cold nor melt in the summer heat.

So the water overflowed and lifted the ark, and it was carried on the surface of the waters. The water had good reason to overflow, when the floodgates of heaven were opened and fountains of water and rivers burst out of the earth. This is said with great emphasis. For where there is a bursting forth, the outpouring cannot be called back, and the onrush of huge streams is not easily held back. What is written, then, is plain. But if you think it should be looked at more deeply, our flesh is tossed by various passions and heaves like a strait at sea; they throw it this way and that, as if on the waves of its own troubles: now by hunger, now by thirst, now by desire, now by joy, now by grief.

I think this too should not be passed over, since Scripture did not pass it over: how many cubits the water stood above the earth. For it said that the water was fifteen cubits above the high mountains. The plain sense is obvious, but the allegory takes in the five senses. In our body they are like high mountains, which overshadow this flesh of passions; they are often overrun by wild beasts, and their dense, dark thickets are disturbed. Hence the Lord too, coming to his Church through the faith of the believing nations, came from Lebanon, as the prophet Habakkuk says: The Lord will come from Lebanon, from a shady and dark mountain. The Church too comes from Lebanon, as the Song of Songs has it. For this is what we read: Come here from Lebanon, my bride, come here from Lebanon. You will pass on and pass through from the beginning of faith, from the lions' dens and the leopards' mountains. These are the Gentile peoples who once suffered, as it were, the grievous onslaughts of bestial passions, and who now stand out in the loftiness of their faith and the sublimity of their devotion. So Christ came through these mountains, curbing the impulses of this fierce body by the teaching of the Gospel, and destroying that loftiness of heart and self-exalting pride by his own obedience and humility. And rightly did those whom the floods of grievous passions had once overwhelmed begin to bear the fruits of gentleness. As for the number of cubits, some before us have reckoned it thus: the five senses are grouped threefold, in that sight sees what is visible, hearing hears what is audible, smell smells what has odor, taste tastes what can be tasted, and touch touches whatever by its substance is subject to touch. So the five senses are reckoned threefold, or else in keeping with that saying: Write it down for yourself threefold. I, however, think it more fitting to take them as the senses of the earthly man, the natural man and the spiritual man, all of which those floodwaters rose above.

[?] All flesh that moved died. This is clear according to the letter, and Scripture has properly and naturally expressed the corruption of the flesh by pointing to a stormy agitation. For agitation is not sinful except through the corruption of the affections: the flesh stirs up pleasures and is itself stirred by pleasures, and such agitation produces corruption. The cause of corruption, then, is the agitation of this world, through which each person's soul degenerates. For when sinful passions move the mind, corruption is produced; when zeal for the virtues is aroused, discipline makes progress. So everyone who was on dry land died, for those whom the waves of so great a flood had submerged could not but die. This is according to what is written and the sequence of the words. But if you look for the allegory, there is no doubt that the soul is like very dry wood, which the fire burns up as soon as it begins to lick at it. Unless the soul is moistened with the dew of the various virtues, watered as by a cup of wisdom, by the fountain of justice and by the stream of chastity, it is burnt up in the fire of desires as though its vital root had withered, or else it is struck down by the flood of the flesh and falls. Therefore the mind ought always to feast on thoughts of good works, so that, made drunk with the juice of prudence, it may grow rich and not easily give way to the assault of the bodily flood, or die unmanned by the dryness and decay of neglect. And so the Lord warns us not to withdraw from the fountain of wisdom but to drink the cups of virtue, so that no one may wither under the sun of iniquity and be unable to withstand the storm of persecution. For it is written: If they do this when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?

God blotted out, it says, everything that was on the face of the earth. The explanation of the text is evident, but the allegory makes it clear that what is set before us is pride. Pride exalts itself in this earthly and fragile substance, forgets divine things, despises human ones, and disfigures the very bearing and gait of the arrogant man. Isaiah describes the daughters of Judah like this, flashing nods of their eyes and tossing their heads on necks held high. For there are people of this kind who raise their eyebrows, with puffed-up heart, swelling chest and head thrown back. They barely graze the ground with the soles of their feet, but poise themselves with their whole body and hang as if on an empty balance. They step forward while tilting their heads backward; they gaze at the sky but disdain the earth, as though their necks were fixed stiff with pain so that they cannot bend them. These, then, God blotted out of the book of life, saying: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled. Nor does he let them, with their fabrications, cleave to heavenly things among the merits of the saints.

So when all who were outside the ark had been killed, Noah alone was left in the ark with those who were with him. The simpler statement needs no interpretation, since the understanding runs together with the letter. But the higher and inner meaning shows the righteous man and lover of wisdom as a fruitful tree. Once the things that used to gnaw at its fruit, overshadow its leaves and cramp the growth of its branches had been destroyed, he remained alone with his own, having no share in irrational passions. "His own" are the pure deliberations of the mind that cling to virtue. And Scripture rightly added that he remained in the ark, as though it seemed scarcely credible that, with the bodily passions cut away, he was still living in the body. For although he was now free of earthly contagion, he still kept the substance of the body, though uncorrupted. He was borne above the flood like one without a body while in the body, and was not swallowed up. He did indeed carry a body, placed as it were inside the ark, yet he was one who, as though without a body, steered that body, unconquerable by passions, through the midst of such great upheavals.

The Lord remembered Noah and the beasts and the cattle, as divine Scripture says. Many people are puzzled about why the writer did not say that God also remembered Noah's wife and sons, when he remembered the beasts and the cattle. But since he said that God remembered Noah, he included the rest of his kin in the founder and head of the household. At the same time a certain harmony among the rest of the family seems to be expressed. For when all are dear to one another, the household is one; but when they are at odds, they are separated and split into many households. Where there is love, then, the whole household is signified by the name of the eldest, on whom the rest depend. In the same way, if someone says "tree" he certainly includes the branches too, and if someone names a branch, he takes in the fruit on it as well, in one and the same word.

Nor is it without purpose that the text says first that God remembered Noah, then the beasts, and after that the cattle. That is, why did it name the fiercer animals after man rather than the gentler ones? The reason seems to be that the fiercer animals might be tamed by being close to both sides. This seems to be stated also in that line of poetry: "and he drove the cowards into the middle." For the poet took this from here too, arranging an army about to fight so that he placed the weaker men in the middle, where they would be helped all the more by the stronger on either side and would join in the fighting of both. Thus the sequence of the text is made plain. In a higher sense, however, it is certain that the righteous man keeps the thoughts of his heart in the middle, not to one side, and as long as he lives this life he must keep grievous beasts in the body, as in that ark. For there is no mind, no soul, that does not admit the wild impulses of evil thoughts as well. So the soul of the fool sharpens savage impulses and stirs up the poisons of serpents, while the strength of the wise man soothes and restrains them.

And the Lord brought a spirit upon the earth, and the water ceased. I do not think this was said in such a way that we should take "spirit" to mean wind. For wind could not dry up the flood. Otherwise, since the sea is stirred up by winds every day, it would surely be emptied. For how could the sea not be drained by the force of the winds, if a flood spread over the whole world, all the way to the Pillars of Hercules, as they say, a great sea surging over the drowned peaks of lofty mountains, had given way to them? There is no doubt, then, that the flood was held back by the invisible power of the divine Spirit, by a heavenly working, not by a blast of wind. Hence it is written: All things wait for you to give them food in due season. When you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness; but when you turn away your face, they will be troubled. You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth. There is, then, a Spirit to whose working all things are seen to yield, in whom lies the power of heaven itself, as it is written: By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth. This Spirit is the creator of all things, as Job also says: The divine Spirit, who made me.

Now let us consider what Scripture means when it says: The fountains of the waters and the floodgates of heaven were shut. I do not think it is obscure. For the flood is reduced by the same causes by which it grew. The fountains of the waters had burst forth and the floodgates of heaven had been opened, so that the earth was inundated by waters flowing in from every side. The sources from which the flood had sprung had to be shut so that it could begin to subside. That is what the letter says. But a subtler interpretation shows that the flood had poured into the soul through the vice of the mind and the luxury of the body, so that malice was mixed with passion and passion with malice. When the physician, the Word of God, comes in to visit the soul, which was suffering from a long illness through the wickedness of its reasonings and the bitterness of its passions, the causes of the sickness first had to be cut away. For the first principle of medicine is to cut off the causes of illness, so that whatever does harm is no longer supplied to make the sickness worse. The law teaches us this too. For when leprosy has come to a halt and no longer spreads, the law says that this halting and stillness of the leprosy is clean, since whatever moves contrary to nature is unclean. This, then, is the health of the soul and the soundness of the mind: that the flood of error should cease and guilt be stopped from spreading. When the spur to guilt and sin ceases, salvation is secure and the soul's vigor flows back unharmed.

And the ark rested, it says, in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month. Unless you pay close attention, this passage is hard to understand even according to the letter. First of all, we must take care that no one is confused by the repeated mention of the seventh month. For it is written that the flood began in the six hundredth year, in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, and that the waters poured in for a hundred and fifty days. The ark rested on a mountain in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month. Afterwards, by God's mercy, the waters began to go down, and they took a hundred and fifty days to decrease. After that the tops of the mountains appeared. Then, after forty days, holy Noah opened the door of the ark. The raven he sent out did not return. The dove he sent out came back empty. Sent out again after seven days, it came back with an olive branch. Sent out a third time after seven days, it did not return, and then Noah realized that all the water had receded. And so the year is shown to end in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month [and so the year is shown to end in Noah's six hundred and first year, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month]. As for the plain explanation, the earth is restored to its proper state after the flood in the same month and on the same day on which it was ruined when the flood began to pour in. For in springtime every field is green and the earth brings forth fruit; then trees begin to bud and fruit to sprout. So the Lord renewed the earth and restored its rich condition. The flood began, then, in the second month, that is, April. For the first month is March, in which the righteous man has his birthday, when the nights and days are reckoned equal: on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, as the Romans think, or as others hold, on the fifth. In the second month, I say, that is April, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the flood began. So spring is reckoned the beginning of the year, not by the customary reckoning of time but by the privilege of nature: since the hope of the year begins then and the fruit begins to show itself, that seems to be the year's beginning. The seventh month, by number, is reckoned to be the one called September. Although the year seems to begin from the month of September, as the use of the present indictions shows (for that is when seed is sown), the origin of the year is really derived from spring, from which a fuller grace begins to show itself. And so the month that by one reckoning is thought to be the first is held by another to be the seventh. It was then, therefore, that the ark rested, in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, upon the mountain of Ararat [?]. From that point the flood began to subside. Notice too that things are undone by the same numbers with which they begin. The flood began in the second month of the year, on the twenty-seventh day of the month. For a hundred and fifty days the flood poured in, and for another hundred and fifty days it gave way. For forty days its overwhelming force surged with rain from heaven and the bursting of the fountains, and when another forty days had passed after the mountain tops were seen, on the first day of the eleventh month, holy Noah sent out the raven. So it is clear that the flood was reduced by the same number by which it had been heaped up. Hence Scripture teaches us that order must be kept.

What the door of the ark is, the door the righteous man opened, has been explained above in its bodily sense. In a higher interpretation, however, it seems we should say that the senses of the body are like doors. Through them, as through doors, a kind of grasp of the things we perceive enters our mind. Our mind, then, seems to look out through these senses, and above all through sight, which is reckoned the most excellent of all the bodily senses because it is akin to light. Through sight we look upon the sky, the earth and the seas, and also the sun, the moon and the stars that adorn the heavens, and we understand that God is the maker and ruler of the world. We believe that these things could not have come into being, nor could they continue to exist, without God as their author and the founder of such great works.

It was through this window, then, that the righteous man first sent out the raven. We must look for the reason, though it is not hidden as far as the letter is concerned: many regard the raven as a kind of herald of things to come, and they watch for its cries and study its flights. The higher sense, however, signifies that the mind of the righteous man, when it begins to cleanse itself, first drives away from itself whatever is dark, unclean and reckless. All shamelessness and guilt is dark and feeds on the dead, as the raven does, whereas virtue is close to light and shines with the purity and simplicity of the mind. And so guilt is, as it were, sent out, put to flight and separated from innocence, so that nothing dark may remain in the mind of the righteous man. Then the raven, once it has gone out, does not return to the righteous man, because all guilt shuns equity and is plainly not in harmony with uprightness and justice. Indeed, the unjust man, who is at home in a kind of flood and corruption, believes he has escaped as if from chains when the righteous man has separated himself from his company. He is like the raven, which found dry land nowhere and yet did not return, but stayed out.

We must also consider why Scripture said that the raven did not return until the water dried from the earth, as if it did return afterward. But this is a customary way of speaking in divine Scripture. In the Gospel, too, you have it written of holy Mary that Joseph did not know her until she bore a son, though he certainly did not know her afterward either. Next, what kind of expression is this, that it said 'until the water dried from the earth' and not 'the earth from the water'? Ordinary usage, it is true, commonly allows this too. Nevertheless some before us have thought that this turn of phrase seems to express a certain unrestrained force of the passions: the soul is consumed by turbulent and stormy passions, but when they fail and, as it were, dry up, it recovers its strength. So the form of guilt does not return into the soul of the righteous man, but leaves that soul behind as something dry and dead, which it can no longer harm.

Nor is it meaningless that the dove is sent out afterward, for simplicity undoes malice and virtue undoes guilt. Malice, then, loves the flood.
