It flees the company of a righteous mind and remains as if desolate and without any resting place, having no fellowship with virtue. Virtue, however, returns, because it loves the company of the righteous and is more at home in bestowing benefit, bringing what leads to salvation and warning against what will do harm and must be avoided. So the dove, when it was sent out and saw that the water had ceased, returned as though full of justice, to tell the one who had sent it what he still needed to beware of, and so that by waiting he might later obtain a better fruit. That the dove, finding no rest, returns to him gives a clear sign that birds of this kind express how great the difference is between malice and virtue. For the raven, sent out earlier, when the flood seemed to be overflowing somewhat more, appeared to have found a place to settle. And certainly the raven is not like other birds that are used to living on the waters. Since, then, the raven seems to have found a place to stay while the dove did not, the evident reason, in a higher interpretation, is this. Malice is accustomed to mingle with the restless passions and desires by which the soul is corrupted; it delights in them as in its kin and household and sets up its dwelling there. Virtue, by contrast, offended at the very first sight, hastened to return to the mind and soul of the righteous man, because a most secure lodging is set for it there, since elsewhere virtue of this kind, like the dove, cannot find so secure a resting place. For simplicity is slow to find a harbor amid the cunning of this world and the waves of worldly desires.

And so, just as virtue goes out a little way as if to pay a visit, then hastens to return to the best of minds and does not go far from the righteous man, so too the righteous man, devoted to virtue, opens wide the bosom of his mind when he perceives that virtue is drawing near. For what is meant by Noah, a man devoted to virtue, stretching out his hand, taking the dove and bringing it in to himself? Though this seems plain according to the letter, you will not easily grasp it unless you know the habit of the wise man. He uses virtue as a kind of scout and seems to entrust to it a certain prerogative in exploring and carrying out affairs. This virtue, then, weighs the natures of others, so that if any of them seems suited to it, it can help it to advance. For the goodness of wisdom is something shared, generous and lavish in its benefits, so that it joins to itself those it sees to be compliant. But when it sees that someone's nature kicks against its purpose, it flies back and hurries home as if to a familiar lodging. The wise and diligent man hastens to receive it as with a kind of hand of the mind, opening his whole heart, in which he held it even while it was absent; for the wise man can never be without his own virtue.

What else is meant by his keeping the dove another seven days and sending it out again, if not that you should notice that the good and excellent purpose of the wise man always seeks to join others to itself as well, to amend those who go astray and correct those who wander? If he sees someone recoil at first, he still does not despair of changing and correcting him. A good physician, even if it is not yet time for medicine, first sends ahead a visit to observe; then he does not neglect to keep watch in due expectation, and, yielding to the disease for a while, waits for the opportunity to heal; and when it is offered, he does not fail in his duty. In the same way the wise man desires to cure the passions opposed to him with words and discussions, as a physician does with medicines. And because in all things we must make use of the remedy of divine favor, he waited seven days, the days in which the whole world is described as having been completed and rest granted to its Maker, so that the discipline of human activity might be learned from him, the author of all things.

So the dove returned toward evening, holding an olive leaf and a twig in its mouth. It was not idly that Scripture put 'evening', 'returned', and 'holding an olive leaf and a twig in its mouth'. It was so that you would not think that virtue shuns future progress, if it can win any, nor again suppose that it had been without light and hidden in some darkness. Rather, shining with the brightness of day, it waited until the day's setting and so returned to him with whom it could have no darkness even in the evening. The leaf too that it brought with it, though it seems to have brought only a small leaf, signified some hope, if not a great one, for those who might repent of their error; for a leaf could not exist without a shoot. So it carried a sign of correction beginning to sprout, as it were—not a great sign, yet a sign. It was an olive leaf, from the tree on which the olive grows; from the olive oil is made, and oil feeds this material light and puts the obscurity of darkness to flight. And what is more akin to virtue than light? The leaf and twig, then, are a sign of correction, and correction has repentance as its root, so to speak. Repentance cannot sprout among the turbulent, but only in those who have already received the spiritual word. Nor is it for nothing that the olive twig is carried in the mouth. Virtue and wisdom have their splendor in speech, and their light shines out at the very first sight, especially when they speak words of peace, since those who seek peace customarily hold out this twig as well. The dove brought a twig because simplicity, through its purity and sincerity, pours seeds of benefit into our ears. The teaching of good virtue either rouses to perseverance and invites to the reward that belongs to one conscious of good discipline, or instils in the sinner the desire to do penance and to follow a new way of life.

Next, it seems we should consider how holy Noah knew that the water had abated from the earth, as it is written. First of all, according to the letter, he could tell whether the leaf it brought was dry or moist; and then, the dove is not the kind of bird that can dig out fruits hidden under water. But you must consider whether that leaf had sprung up before the flood or during it. If before the flood, the righteous man rejoiced that some fruit of the old seed had been preserved, and from this he gathered a sign of divine mercy: that mercy had now removed the flood and was showing a fruit that the floods had been unable to harm. If the leaf was born during the flood, the righteous man surely noticed that new seeds of heavenly mercy had put forth shoots, so that the roots of the trees were alive and, as if they had recovered their life, were sprouting their former offspring and returning to their accustomed bearing, of which the leaves sent on ahead gave evidence.

But he gathered this rather by a deeper interpretation: that the Lord our God, though offended by the bitter errors of our iniquity, nevertheless preserved for us some seed, however small, of our ancient lineage and ancestral virtue, so that every trace of his work and creation in the human race should not be utterly cut off. Hence Isaiah too says: 'Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.' By the name of the one city he expresses a sign of blindness, and by the name of the other barrenness. For the Chaldeans in their native tongue named Sodom and Gomorrah with words meaning blindness and barrenness. And rightly, in the figure of such cities, the Lord cut away human vices rather than judging that men should be punished.

The third time, the dove is sent out after seven days, and it does not come back. Let us consider this, so that what we said above may not turn out to be contradictory. If the dove in word, but virtue in fact, does not return to the righteous man, was the righteous man then abandoned and cheated of his gift? Not at all. Such a man is never separated from virtue. When he sends forth justice from his mouth and opens a discussion of some virtue, he does not strip himself of virtue or rob himself of the equity that others are to imitate; rather, like the sun, he illuminates others when he sends out the rays of his light. Fire, after all, warms those who come near it while keeping the heat of its own nature. Does the light of day fail when it illuminates the whole world with its brightness? It keeps its course unhindered and its nature undiminished. So too this virtue in the figure of the dove: while the flood was still seething, it returned to the righteous man—as a bird, on the earth; as virtue, among the passions of men—because it had not been able to find a place in the hearts of the wicked where it could cling. And so, returning to that second lodging of its own, it clings there and rests. But when the floods of the passions have cooled, and a great many have become eager to share in the word they have heard and the teaching they have learned, then the discipline of virtue begins to be no longer the patrimony of one man but a common good. It is drunk like a cup of wisdom by very many who before, though thirsty, refused to drink. So now the floods seethe in the hearts of the Jews, and though the water of heavenly teaching overflows and drink is abundant, they do not think it should be drunk. The Gospel is read, virtue goes forth from the heavenly word, the priest preaches in the church; but in case, placed alone within the ark, he cannot be heard, he sometimes goes out of the church as well, and wherever he meets a Jew, he admonishes him and brings forward an example from the heavenly Scriptures. They stop their ears, so that the fountain may not wash them even against their will, nor the moisture of the Lord's word sprinkle them. But if any believe, they run to the fountain, they seek the teaching, they long to have the Gospel instilled in them, and they are not sated by drinking constantly. So they eagerly desire to be filled from the fountain of wisdom that before they were eager to flee. What fountain? Hear him saying: 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.'

In the six hundred and first year of Noah's life, on the first day of the first month, Scripture says that the water was diminished from the face of the earth, and it records that in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dried. What does this addition about the diminishing of the water mean, since the reckoning given above seems to have completed the year, a year that begins in the second month and runs on to the second month of the following year? Perhaps we should take it that the figure of the righteous man is declared here. The first year would be the one in which the flood began, that is, the first year after the six hundredth; and again there is a first year and a first month after the six hundredth year, when the water was diminished from the face of the earth. This is because the righteous man was first in virtue in the generation of sinners, which was destroyed for its offenses, and first in order in the second generation, which began after the flood, since he was the first of that second generation. And rightly he had escaped as the first. Honor is rightly paid to him who was both the first of the first generation and the beginning of the later one, who deserved both to escape from the one and to be propagated as the seedbed of the other. For while others perished, he alone, rich before God through the merit of an outstanding life and the prerogative of virtue, did not experience the corruption of malice. Through him it came about that the whole body of the human race neither seemed to be wiped out on earth nor was left cut off from the grace of God.

'And Noah,' it says, 'uncovered the roof of the ark.' Since, as we interpreted above, we have taken the ark as a figure of the body, let us understand what it means to uncover the body, according to the higher sense, that is; for it is plain how the ark could be opened according to the letter. What, then, is the roof of the human body, which was kept closed during the flood? Perhaps we should take it to be pleasure, which covered this body of ours and, as it were, roofed it over because of that error of Adam. And pleasure is thought most like a roof above all because all sensation is in the head, and from there comes pleasure, which held the whole body subject to it. But the mind of the righteous man was sober and untouched by the corruption of the flood, and when, inflamed with desire for the knowledge of God, it wished to leap out and fly up to higher things, it uncovered everything that stood in its way. The form of pleasure, which like a covering roofed over the other parts of the body, it opened up and laid bare, so as not only to free the body from slavery to a base mistress, but also to grasp the things that are incorporeal; for the things that are not seen are eternal. And so the righteous man, free from corruption and longing for eternity, sought the Lord whom he did not see.

As for Scripture's speaking of the first month or the second, and of this as a day in springtime, you have it said elsewhere too: 'This month shall be for you the first among the days of the year.' For he who was first in grace after the danger rightly received the prerogative of the first month.

But do not be troubled that we said above that the leaf found on the branch could have been produced after the flood, even though plants commonly sprout under water. Still, to remove every doubt: what great thing is it if, at God's command, on the very day the water was diminished, the earth at once sprouted, since he is both the restorer and the creator of fruits and had not forgotten how his work functions? Indeed, you have it at the very beginning that he commanded the earth to sprout grass for fodder and the fruit-bearing tree with its fruit—and at once the earth brought forth grass for fodder bearing seed according to its kind, and the fruit-bearing tree—and that it was a single day on which God commanded or made these things. So God, mindful of his kindness but unmindful of our iniquity, restored his work in the same span of time in which he began it.

'And the Lord God said to Noah: Go out of the ark, you and your wife and your sons.' So once the water had receded and the earth was dried, Noah could have gone out of the ark. But the righteous man claims nothing for himself; he commits himself entirely to the divine command. And above all, he who had entered at a heavenly oracle had to wait for a heavenly answer before going out. For justice is modest, whereas iniquity is shameless, usurping what is not its due and showing no reverence for its author.

Now let us ask why, when they were entering the ark, the order of those entering was this: first Noah himself entered and his sons, then his wife and his sons' wives; but when they went out, the order was changed. For it is written: 'He went out, and his wife and his sons and his sons' wives.' The letter, indeed, signifies abstinence from begetting at the entrance and the practice of begetting at the exit. For then the father went in first with his sons, and the sons with their father, and after them his wife and his sons' wives; that is, the sexes are not mingled at the entrance, but they are mingled at the exit. So by the very order of entering, the righteous man openly sends out a kind of message: that was no time for intercourse or pleasures, when destruction hung over everyone. Hence the Lord in the Gospel says, by way of reproach, that in the days of Noah they ate and drank, married wives and gave their daughters in marriage, and that therefore, because of their intemperance, the flood came upon them. That was a time of mourning, then, not of rejoicing, and so the righteous man took no pleasure in the company of his wife, nor did his sons seek conjugal union. For how unseemly it would be, at a time when the living were dying, for those destined to perish to be begotten! Afterward, however, when the flood receded, the practice and care of marriage rightly followed, to provide seed for the rest. And so men do not go out with men, but women with men, so that the union of male with male might be seen to be forbidden, while the union of male and female in the lawful lot of marriage is permitted.

The higher sense, however, holds this: where there is danger, manly and stronger reasonings should cling to the mind, and the mind should protect itself with them as with a kind of offspring of sons, so that a manly battle line, as it were, may meet the storms and the more grievous passions. But once the danger has passed, there is no harm if softer thoughts are joined to stronger ones—not so that the stronger may be made effeminate by the softer, but so that the softer thoughts may be strengthened by manly ones, as it were. For all our counsels are directed toward virtue, justice, integrity and fortitude, and through a kind of practice and seedbed of virtue stronger counsels can be produced and grow. It is not useful, then, when some turmoil of vices occupies the mind, to sow thoughts or for the mind to beget and give birth. But when desires have been suppressed and the mind has come to rest, then, having received a kind of seed of reasoning, virtues and good works can sprout.

'And Noah,' it says, 'built an altar to God.' Someone may perhaps ask why, when above the Lord had instructed him what to do and Noah did everything, he now did this without being instructed. But surely the Lord should not, like a miser, demand payment for his grace, and the righteous man understood that true thanksgiving is the kind that is not commanded but freely offered. And so he allowed no delay either; for the grateful virtue of the soul shuts out the weakness of hesitation, while one who owes thanks and waits for them to be demanded of him is ungrateful. And as for its saying he built the altar to God—not to the Lord, but to God—according to the meaning of the name, this thanksgiving seems not to have been forced, as if paid to a Lord, but to have come from the willing and grateful virtue of the righteous man.

Addressing him as God, as it were, he set aside the name that speaks of command and used the name that speaks of kindness. 'And he took of the clean beasts and of the clean birds,' it says, 'and offered burnt offerings.' The letter makes it plain that we ought to offer what is undefiled, things in which the devotion of the one offering may shine. The higher interpretation, however, holds that the clean beasts are the senses of the wise man, and the birds his powers of understanding, which are far subtler and lighter.

Now let us consider more carefully what it means when it says that the Lord God, reflecting, said: "I will not again curse the earth because of the works of men, for the heart of man remains diligently set on evil from his youth. I will not, then, again strike all flesh, as I have done, for all the days of the earth." Although he had taken vengeance on the human race, he nevertheless knew that the punishment of the law serves to produce fear and an understanding of his teaching, rather than to change nature, which can be corrected in some but cannot be changed in all. So the Lord punished so that we might fear, and he spared so that we might be preserved. He punished once, as an example to inspire fear; he spared for the time to come, so that the bitterness of sin should not rule for ever, and also because anyone who wants to punish sins too often is thought harsh rather than just. And so God says: "I will not again curse the earth because of the works of men." That is, since he wished to show his goodness toward all mankind, and yet ought not to bring a kind of careless complacency into human minds, he punishes a few and preserves the many. Then, when he says, "I will not again," he shows that he lightens rather than increases the hardships of men, knowing that the sins of men cannot be entirely removed. As the proverb has it, trying to rid the hearts of men of wickedness is like trying to draw water with a fine net.

"I will not again," he says, "curse the earth because of the sins of men, for the mind of man remains diligently set on evil from his youth." See how God indicates that we sin with zeal, by saying that the mind of man remains diligently set on evil. By this he seems to indicate that the heart of man leans diligently toward sin, that there is in our ruling part a slipperiness toward sinning, and, what is worse, that eagerness for it is not lacking. That is why he says "diligently," as though we were anxious that freedom from guilt might not creep up on us. Then he did not speak of one evil but of many evils, and he added "from his youth," for wickedness grows from that age. We do indeed read elsewhere that not even an infant one day old is without sin; but infancy is not without sin because of the weakness of the body, whereas diligence and eagerness in sinning begin in youth. So a child sins as one who is weak, but a young man as one who is wicked, who eagerly desires to commit sins and glories in his crimes; for many people count innocence as cowardice and guilt as something to be praised. Thus young men have grown used to boasting of their luxury, their pleasures and their adulterous passions. Guilt, then, grows with age. So he declares that the whole human race is no longer to be destroyed when he says, "I will not again strike all flesh"; instead, punishment is reserved for a part.

What, too, is the meaning of his saying: "Seed and harvest, cold and heat, summer and spring, by day and by night, shall not cease"? According to the letter, it signifies that as long as the seasons remain as the Lord established them and keep their proper state, the animals and all growing things will remain and will be uncorrupted. For when the seasons are corrupted, the things that are produced each in their own season are corrupted too. If there is confusion of the seasons, how can the things that bring forth survive once that confusion has occurred? So it is the seasons that either corrupt or preserve, according to the quality they themselves have. And so the year is made up of contraries: spring, autumn, summer and winter. Just as the harmony of a song seems to consist in the blending of low and high notes, so also this world is held together by contraries: air and earth, fire and water. Our bodies too maintain a certain order of nature through cold and heat, moisture and dryness. For if the natural order and measure is thrown into confusion, destruction must follow. So the Lord, having removed the confusion of the flood, promises that there will be a fixed order of the seasons for the preservation of the world.

The deeper sense, however, is this: by seed we are to understand the beginning, and by harvest the end. In both lies the cause of salvation. One without the other is incomplete, for it is said: "Where there is a beginning, an end is sought; nor can there be a beginning if the end is taken away, and the end runs back into the beginning." So he records that the human race, as long as it is in this world, will always return to the same things, so that when the year begins it comes to an end, and when it ends it begins again, and the world is not dissolved in the middle of its course. So too the mind, when it seems to begin something, should press on to the end and seek the completion of its work. When it finishes some work, it should not take a holiday as though the work were done, but should return to other works and always practise growth in virtue, since it sees that the earth is always called back to bearing its fruits, which come forth at different times, either in spring and

summer, as in the eastern regions, or in summer and autumn, as in the western regions. At one season the seeds of the earth bring forth their offspring; at another we gather the fruits of the trees. So fruits are divided into necessary and pleasurable: the necessary come from the seeds of the earth, the pleasurable from the fruits of the trees. And so our body is fed with natural food as in spring, that is, in ἔαρ; ἔαρ is the Greek name, and in Latin it is called uer. Therefore Scripture took its example from the eastern regions, and especially from Egypt, through which the Hebrew passed, or else from the regions of Phoenicia. The soul, however, is nourished by the pleasurable fruits, that is, the fruits of wisdom. And just as cold and heat are contrary to our body, so fear and anger seem to be hostile to the soul. But because it is in the body, it must have both anger and fear, and it cannot be without them, owing to the necessity of bodily nature.

And therefore the mind of the wise man distributes just measures, so that he does not mix anger and fear together and produce a kind of confusion and flood in his soul. As for his saying "by day and by night," by day you understand illuminating virtue, and by night you recognize the darkness of folly. So even in fear, as in cold, there can be illuminating virtue. Likewise temperance can restrain anger, so that one is not utterly undone by fear but is instead directed by fear toward the works of virtue. For example, if a persecutor presses upon you, you should fear God more and think that everlasting punishments are to be avoided more than present ones; and while you fear these, you should be kindled to glory, angry at faithlessness and at crime; and again, when you are inflamed with anger, you should moderate your agitation by the fear of God.

"And the Lord blessed Noah and his sons, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and rule over it. And the fear and dread of you shall be upon all the beasts of the earth and upon all the birds of the sky, and upon all that move on the earth and upon all the fish of the sea." This prerogative of power over the other animals appears to have been granted to man in the earlier passages as well, in the place where it says that God made man in the image of God; there it says: "Male and female he made them, and he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and rule over it, and have power over the fish of the sea and the birds and the beasts of the earth and the creeping things." I have pointed this out so that you may understand that a twofold generation of man is expressed: one according to the image of God, the other according to the shaping from the clay of the earth. Indeed, that creation of man from the clay of the earth seems to have taken place after the world was made, after God had rested from his works. The fashioning of an earthly statue is produced, as it were, late. There was no rain on the earth, and no man worked the earth. Then God formed man from the slime of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul. But the man who was established on the sixth day, as by a perfect number in which all the works of God were completed, as by a perfect work, was made according to the image of God. To him is compared also this man who was found righteous in the flood. And therefore God set him above all earthly things, just as he did the one made in the image of God, because each kept himself free from earthly vices: the one because he was so generated that he owed nothing to earthly contagion, the other because he had been proved in dangers and tested in sufferings, and found

not to have been subject to confusion in the midst of confusion. The deeper sense, however, is that the righteous man is increased by the greatness and abundance of virtue and of learning, and fills the earth, which is like a heart in which there is a store of intelligible things. Thus he allows nothing to be empty of wisdom, which folly could invade. He rules, therefore, over all earthly passions, and also over the bodily senses; he also subdues to himself through a kind of terror and fear the beasts, in which there seems to be an image of malice and savagery. For all malice is harsh and wild; it swells with a kind of airy swelling. Nor is it obscure that certain creeping things bear a likeness to deadly passions, from which a kind of poison seems to be poured into the mind. Over all these, then, the righteous man rules; he does not mingle with them but restrains them, provided his mind is not led by pleasure or by desire, is not broken by sorrow and fear, and does not run the course of this life, slippery and fleeting as it is, in luxury and pleasures. Instead, the wise man banishes such passions from himself by self-control and temperance.

But since he immediately adds, "All creeping things that are alive shall be food for you," in case it troubles you that we spoke earlier of poisonous creeping things, understand that some creeping things are poisonous and others harmless. Take this, then, of the harmless creeping things, which, although they do not all creep on belly and breast like snakes, still have small feet, so that they seem to creep rather than walk. So take the unclean bodily passions as being like the poisonous creeping things, and the seemly ones as being like the harmless. For every affection that is free from the allurement of shameful pleasure is indeed a passion, but a good passion. Softer desire, anger and fear: these are harmful passions of the soul; but harmless affections are good passions. Through these a certain way and reason of living is supplied to us; we use them as food for the enjoyment of life; we delight in them as in a feast.

What, too, is the meaning of his saying: "As the green herbs of the field, I have given you all things"? On this point even those who understand simply, without weighing the precise sense of the words, do not seem to us to be opposed. For there are some who think that green herbs appear to have been assigned to us as food by God's command, so that we ought to use them rather than meat dishes. For my part I would gladly agree with them, so that the use of vegetables might become established in the human race for the sake of thrift and temperance, were it not that I see that those who do not willingly accept this could reply to me that not all green herbs are found suitable as human food, and further that not every kind of person is led by love of wisdom and self-control so as to be able to pursue self-control. And therefore we cannot narrow a general precept to the small portion of a few people; for this precept is given to all people.

Let us therefore consider what he said: "As the green herbs of the field, I have given you all things." He did not say, "I have given you all green herbs for food." So let those who eat meat use it as they would green herbs, not to distend the body or fatten it, as meat dishes usually do. But just as not all green herbs are fit to be used as food, so too not every living creeping thing is suitable for eating, since we ought to abstain from all poisonous ones. Yet luxury has gone so far that it considers pleasure more than danger, and in many cases, after cutting away the part that is said to be naturally poisonous, it claims the remaining part for food. Even if this is not full of danger, it is still close to danger, and some corruption must have spread into the juice of the whole flesh. Many people also shoot deer and swift animals of that kind with poisoned arrows, and afterwards, having cut away a certain part of the limbs, use the rest of the body for food.

As for the deeper sense, that is, the reason why it was chiefly said: irrational passions ought to be subject to the mind of the wise man as green herbs are to a countryman, and he should use them, as creeping thoughts, just as a farmer uses green herbs, which cannot do harm but do not have the satisfaction of more solid food. For a precept that is general and common to all does not impose the higher kinds of virtue, which in any case belong to few. But even if someone cannot provide himself with the more solid feasts of the virtues, let him at least have passions of a kind that do no harm but give delight.

That is why holy Moses at the beginning taught and instructed us about the breathing in of the soul, so that we would not slip into the various opinions of the philosophers, who cannot agree even with themselves. Many of them held differing views: Critias and his disciples, for instance, said that the soul is blood—meaning, of course, this soul by which we live, which is the sensitive soul, not that soul which is held to be the rational and intelligent soul of the inner man. Hippocrates, though he did not disapprove of Critias's ingenuity or refute his argument, nevertheless did not agree with his opinion. Aristotle called it entelechy; others held it to be fire. Let us, then, keep to this division: we should distinguish the rational part of the soul, whose substance is the divine Spirit, as Scripture says, "for he breathed into his face the breath of life"; and in the soul there is also a certain life-giving nourishment by which this body is animated, and there is also a part that feels pleasure. Some call the substance of these life-giving and pleasure-feeling parts of the soul blood, since Scripture too said: "The soul of all flesh is its blood." So it was properly that he called blood the soul of the flesh; for in the flesh are pleasure and passion, not mind and reasoning. Yet if you attend carefully, this passage explains that one. For when he called blood the soul in this place, he certainly indicated that the soul is one thing and blood another, so that the substance of the soul is the vital breath, yet this vital breath does not supply the ability to live on its own and without blood, but is mingled with the blood. For there are the so-called arteries, which are receptacles of the breath, as it were, and contain not only pure air but also blood, though a far smaller portion of blood. For there are two kinds of vessels: one is the veins, called φλέψ in Greek, the other the arteries. The vein, that is, φλέψ, has more blood than breath; the artery has less blood and much more breath. The proportion, moreover, varies according to the differing nature of individual people.

The deeper sense, however, ought to delight you. It signifies that blood was called the soul because blood is warm and fiery, as virtue is. Whoever, then, has been kindled with zeal for virtue and has taken on the glow of praise shuts out all the delights of the belly. "So you who are set in the ardour of virtue," he says, "will reject those thoughts that are carnal and earthly as unfit for spiritual food." For he was not eating flesh—that is, he was not thinking of anything earthly—who said, "My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven," breathing into men zeal for virtue and pouring into them a longing for the knowledge of God. So earthly and feeble thoughts are considered as though unmanned and without the use of blood, just as a man is said to be unmanned when he has lost a great deal of blood, for with the shedding of blood he grows cold. Whoever, then, is diligent in the virtues banishes and rejects bodily foods, except as much as he knows is enough for nature; but whoever is more careless and has followed the slippery and watery course of this life loses his footing, as it were, and falls into his belly and stomach. So the man who is a stranger to heavenly food, and who cannot say, "But our citizenship is in heaven," desires earthly things. And so, to call us to foods set apart, the same apostle says: "Do not touch, do not defile, do not taste, things which by their very use lead to corruption, according to the precepts and doctrines of men; things which indeed have an appearance of wisdom in the observance of religion and humility of heart, not in indulgence of the body, not in any honour paid to the satisfying and pampering of the flesh."

Finally, what follows confirms that this is the sense, for it says: "For I will require your blood and that of your souls from all the beasts and from the hand of man." He compared man's wickedness to the malice of beasts—indeed he heaped it up beyond the savagery of beasts—by saying, "from the hand of a man's brother." For beasts have nothing of nature in common with us; they are bound by no brotherly bond. If they harm men, they harm them as strangers; they do not violate the laws of nature or forget the affection of kinship. Therefore a man sins more gravely when he plots against his brother, and therefore the Lord promised that he would punish more severely, saying: "I will require the blood of man from the hand of his brother." Or is he not a brother whom a kind of womb of rational nature has brought forth, and to whom birth from the same mother has joined us? For the same nature is the mother of all men, and so we are all brothers, born of one and the same mother and bound by the same law of kinship.

And so the Lord also used the word "brother," and called him a brother from whom a brother's blood is required. By this he indicates that danger is rather to be feared from those who are joined to us by a brother's bond. For it is from this quarter that plots, from this quarter that dangers, are more often devised against men. To take a particular case, hatreds often spring up between brothers in the strict sense when an inheritance is divided. Then, if a brother has been given more by his parents, the other brothers are especially indignant and try to take away by murder the favour the parents have bestowed. These are the wars most to be suspected—wars not between cities but within individual households. So the Lord has included in the judgement of vengeance those he knew would be more likely to plot against one another.

The third point is that he used the word "brother" not because a murderer of his kin deserves a name of devotion, but so that he might be more heavily burdened by the name of devotion, and so the crime might be increased by it, making the heavenly punishment more just. So the Lord our God promises vengeance, so that at least in this way the one who has forgotten devotion may be broken by fear, and may know that even if the murderer escapes men, he cannot escape the judgement of God, but is reserved for a greater and eternal punishment.

In a deeper sense, however, we understand this: we must be on our guard not only against plots from strangers but also from our own, that is, from the thoughts of our own household; and further, we must watch ourselves not only against malice of mind but also against our own words. And so it says: "In much speaking you will not escape sin." So this seems to be what is signified: that we must render account to the Lord not only for our deeds but also for our speech, which is even closer to home. And therefore we must consider very carefully that we do not incur offence either by word or by deed, because just as confession is made with the mouth to salvation, so with the mouth a fall is made to death.

"Whoever sheds the blood of man," it says, "for the blood of man his own shall be shed." The expression is not a mistake; rather, the words carry emphasis, meaning that whoever sheds the blood of man shall himself be poured out like blood, which robs him of the hope of posterity. For just as blood poured on the ground is scattered this way and that, so the soul of the wicked is dissolved in the manner of bodily frailty. For it was also said of the soul that its death is corruption, because it is cheated of the gift of heavenly grace and, as though dashed on the rocks of wickedness, it wastes away the body of its health.

Many people are also troubled that he said, "I made man in the image of God," and did not say, "in my image," since he himself is God. But understand that there is both a Father and a Son. And although all things were made through the Son, we nevertheless read that the Father made all things and made them through the Son, as it is written: "In wisdom you have made all things." So if it is the Father who speaks, he made man in the image of the Word; if it is the Son who speaks, he made him in the image of God the Father. And therefore he shows that the nature of man—that is, of rational man, according to which we were created in the image of God—is in a sense familiar and close to God, as one of his own household; and for that reason what he sees cruelly and wickedly done against a creature of his own household does not go unpunished before God.

So the reason added for the punishment serves first to rule out the opinions of certain philosophers who deny that God takes care of men; and then, knowing that the prerogative of avenging us rests with God, we should neither commit against others what is to be punished by divine judgement, nor ourselves fear death too greatly, since we know that the killing of an innocent man is in no way disregarded by God.

"There shall not be a flood," it says, "to destroy the whole earth." There seems to be some doubt whether "there shall not be a flood" is to be understood as "a flood that destroys the earth"—for that is what floods usually do—or rather as "there shall not be such a flood as will destroy the whole earth." What follows makes this clear, when it says that the whole earth is not to be destroyed; for it shows that there will indeed be floods, but not such as could destroy the whole earth.

The higher sense contains this: the Lord's providence will now see to it that the flood of bodily passions is not so great that every soul perishes. Yet I do not dare to say that the Lord seems to lay down that no one's soul can utterly perish. For what do we say of the parricide? What of the murderer, the adulterer, the transgressor? What parts of his soul do we keep in reserve for pardon? So I rather think that the Lord our God is urging us on: even if someone has other, lighter passions, he should not utterly despair of divine grace, nor wholly doubt that he will live. Even if he is given to luxury and cannot escape the pursuit of it, let him still strive to keep himself from adultery; let his delight be in feasting, not in debauchery. And even if someone is greedy, has plundered what belongs to others, thrown out orphans and turned widows out of doors, let him at least turn back afterwards in repentance and restore what he took. Zacchaeus, after all, earned pardon because he promised not only to make restitution but to pay back fourfold to those from whom he had taken anything, and also to give half of his property to the poor.

Let us also consider more carefully what he means when he says: "I will set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of an everlasting covenant between me and the earth. And when I gather clouds over the earth, my bow shall appear in the cloud, and I will remember my covenant." For he does not mean, as many think, the bow that people say exists and gives signs of rain. In that bow various colours appear, like rays of the sun now glowing red, now shining with a clearer light, and from it rain to come is foretold, because its many-coloured appearance shows that the fair weather is unsettled. Some call this bow the iris, but far be it from us to say that this is God's bow. For this bow, called the iris, is usually seen by day and does not appear at night. Even by day it is not seen if the sky is overcast with dark clouds, unless perhaps the heavier clouds have begun to break up.

So let us consider whether Scripture, because a bow for shooting arrows is now drawn, now unstrung, may mean a certain tension and relaxation, so that the universe is not utterly broken by excessive tension, but there is a certain measure and a certain balance of divine power. There is, then, an invisible power of God which, like this bow that is drawn and relaxed, governs according to the divine will, mercy and power, and allows all things neither to fall into confusion through excessive slackening nor to be torn apart through excessive bursting. He says it is set in the clouds because the help of divine providence is most needed when the masses of clouds are driven together into storms and tempests. And so he says: "I will set my bow in the cloud," not "I will set my arrow." The bow is the instrument for shooting the arrow, and it is not the bow itself that wounds but the arrow. That is why the Lord sets a bow rather than an arrow in the clouds: not something that wounds, but something that serves as a sign of terror yet does not usually inflict a wound.

Why, when he had earlier counted the three sons of Noah, Shem, Ham and Japheth, does he here include the descendants of only the middle son—that is, when he says: "Ham was the father of Canaan; these were the three sons of Noah"—especially since those two were righteous and this middle one unrighteous? So the descendants of the unrighteous one are mentioned before those of the righteous. We cannot deny what is written, but his descendants were added to heap up his offence: though he had a son and was himself a father, he alone failed to honour his father, he who more than anyone ought to have honoured him. And so he deserved to have a wicked son, because he had been wicked toward his father. At the same time it indicates that the Canaanites came from that Canaan, and after many generations they were crushed by a righteous people and their land passed into its possession. It is clear, then, that the ancestor of the Canaanites was Canaan, the son of this Ham who showed himself impious toward his father.

A higher sense is indicated by the meaning of the names. Ham means "heat," Canaan "their disturbance." Whoever is hot is constantly agitated and disturbed. So it is made perfectly plain that it was not so much a man who was father of men, as an evil passion that gave birth to a wicked passion, one estranged from its father's character, that is, from the practice of virtue.

"And Noah began to be a husbandman of the earth." At first sight Noah, the righteous man, seems comparable to Adam, who was made from the earth. Of Adam it is written that after he was cast out of paradise he began to work the earth, and of Noah that after he came out of the ark he became a husbandman. In both cases a sort of flood had come first: Noah came after the flood, and Adam, as regards the fashioning of his body, after the world was set in order. For in making the world the water was gathered into one place so that the land might appear, which could not be seen before because of the confusion of waters. So as that first-born master is seen to have worked the earth, so Noah too, coming out of the ark, became the founder of sowing and cultivation. These are thought to be alike. But if you consider the words, which already convey the force of a higher sense, it is one thing to be a worker of the earth and another to be a husbandman: the one acts as a hireling, the other as the head of the household. Cain, who killed his brother, was a worker of the earth. And so that you may know that working the earth is more servile than free, the murderer's work is included in the curse. For it is written: "For you shall work the earth, and it shall not increase its strength to give to you. Groaning and trembling you shall be upon the earth."

Now the earth is our flesh. The wicked man works it, but the good man cultivates it. The one seeks wages from the earth, as it were; the other seeks to gather the fruits of goodness and the grace of discipline, so as to make his field more fruitful, able to answer to the Lord's cultivation and display the care of its cultivator. But what does the worker seek except food for his body alone? He is more intent on serving his belly and content to secure only what can help to feed him. The other is nourished by the profit of fruits. You know what fruits the righteous man has: "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, goodness." So the good husbandman has continence and chastity, so that if any trees quickly bend down to the ground and sprout too lavishly, he may cut them back, as with the pruning-hook of his temperance, so that they cast off what is weak and put forth what is comely.

Why is it that the righteous man first plants a vineyard, and not wheat or barley? And where did a vine come from after the flood and the ruin of the earth? We spoke of this above: in springtime even the roots of ruined vines could sprout. So I think the following question must be settled with greater care: why the righteous man seeks first what serves pleasure rather than what is necessary. Wheat and barley are necessary crops, without which we cannot live, whereas wine serves pleasure and was given for enjoyment. Because he was righteous, he claimed this for himself instead, that is, what came second rather than what is first. For the necessary foods of life he offered to God, as being ... [?]

but wine is superfluous for men and not necessary. Perhaps you will say that men cannot live without drink any more than without food. Is drink, then, as necessary as food? I do not deny it. Has the Lord appointed it as necessary for thirst? I do not dispute it. And so for necessary drink it is right to draw from springs and rivers, which were not made by human hands but flowed at the command and by the working of the Lord our God. And because we spoke of the Lord's working, do not twist this back to the point that Cain's working seems to have carried curses. Consider that it is not working that is called cursed, but the fact that it is written "to work the earth." For whoever works the earth is a hireling. But he is not a hireling, he is the Lord, who says: "My Father is working until now, and I am working." Hear what such a worker works at: "My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven."

"And he drank," it says, "of the wine and became drunk." It did not say "he drank wine," nor did the righteous man drain the wine; he drank "of the wine," that is, he tasted a portion of it. It is the drunkard who swallows down all the wine, and the intemperate man who empties whatever he takes; the continent man must keep to a lawful measure. There are two kinds of drunkenness. One makes the body stagger, trips up its steps and confuses its senses; the other fills the mind with the vapour of the grace of virtue and seems to drive away all weakness. Hence the apostle says: "Use a little wine on account of your frequent ailments." For just as wine drunk in this moderation does not cause weakness but brings health and relieves every bodily weakness, so that glorious drunkenness shuts out every weakness of the flesh. Of it is written: "And the cup that inebriates, how glorious it is!" What is this drunkenness? "Do not get drunk," he says, "with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit," as the apostle said. So according to the letter there is a warning, and according to the higher sense there is praise of the wise man. He is cautious who, even if he is stripped, is stripped in his own house, where there is no lack of coverings and of certain veils for drunkenness, so that he knows how to hide his faults.

Bodily coverings, such as walls and roofs, cover the naked body; let us see what the coverings of the soul are. But we will find the coverings only if we have examined the soul's stripping. The stripping of the wise man is twofold. Our mind, then, is clothed with a twofold garment if either it has committed a sin unknowingly—this is the stripping of a mind as if drunk, so that it does not know it is doing wrong, like one who is led into vice by a sort of intoxication of ignorance and slips—or again, buried in the sleep of negligence and ignorance, it does not recognize its error. When we fall into these things—indeed, when we fall into many sins even knowingly, for there is also a natural drunkenness of our weakness, so that we are carried into vice by the rush of pleasure, as many are, kindled by youthful heat, inflamed by luxury and delight, or swept away by the desire of avarice—surely a remedy must be sought for all of these. One should first cover such weakness with a certain shame and modesty, so that even if he still stands on the slippery ground of sin, he may yet give a sign of amendment. For it makes a great difference whether one wishes to flaunt one's sins [?]: in the one case there is shameful impudence, in the other a tolerable modesty that shows hope of future correction.

There is another stripping of the soul, by which it casts off and puts off the body like a kind of burden, escaping as it were from the tomb of the flesh. For the throat of such men is "an open tomb," and in that tomb the soul is buried, so to speak, weighed down by various pleasures and passionate desires. So whatever soul has stripped itself of every snare of the passions and turned away from all that unsightly appearance of earthly stain, so as to see the light of eternal beauty, strips itself of the earthly heap and escapes and flees, as it were, from the nets thrown around it.

Now I ask why he did not simply say, "Ham saw his father's nakedness," but "Ham, the father of Canaan, saw." Canaan had certainly not yet been born. Why then did he add the son's name, unless so that the heir might be disgraced by the fault of his begetter, and the begetter be weighed down by the son's wickedness? Thus the father is convicted in the son and the son in the father, since they share in common folly, wickedness and impiety as well. Nor could he beget a good son who had himself proved a worthless son to a good father, a degenerate both in nature and in upbringing.

So much for the letter. As for the higher sense, all the worst characters delight in the errors of others, and not only in errors but also in things that seem evil to them, even if they are not. For Noah did not perceive that he was naked, since he was clothed with the garment of wisdom. Nor indeed did Adam, placed in paradise, think himself naked until after he had committed the error of transgression. Then, uncovered of the garment of wisdom and justice and stripped by transgressing the heavenly commands, he saw that he was naked and thought he must cover himself with leaves. So Ham laughs when he sees his father stripped. For every wicked man, since he himself strays from discipline, not only takes the falls of others as a consolation for his own error, because he has found partners in guilt, but even rejoices with wicked feeling, as though he had corrected his own faults. So the evil mind rejoices that something has befallen the wise man contrary to his intention, though a bodily slip ought surely not to be counted a vice, even if it is thought a slip, unless the mind too leans toward guilt. Indeed, such errors should be judged pardonable, not pursued with hatred or held up to mockery. But the wicked mind, as I said, when it thinks the wise man has erred, thinks it must insult the one whose character it considers contrary to its own, because its own sin is convicted, as it were, by the silent testimony of the wise man. And so it thinks it must rejoice that the righteous man's learning has not profited him, nor his justice supported him, nor have the things of the body run a prosperous course for him. For among the wicked the highest goods are thought to lie in wealth or honour, which yet contribute no fruit to the praise of virtue. Therefore the defenders of folly, who think every good is to be valued by temporal rather than eternal things, [?] that the lover of virtue has been cheated of the gift of prosperity.

Why is it that Shem and Japheth put a garment upon their shoulders and walked backward and covered their naked father, and did not see his nakedness? The letter expresses a clear feeling of filial devotion: the good sons took care not to see their father stripped of his clothing, so that their reverence for him might not be lessened even by the very sight, since devotion is often wounded even by a silent glance. Hence it is said that at Rome too there was an old custom that sons, especially once grown, should not enter the bath with their parents.

The higher sense contains this: the fool sees only things present, which are before his eyes; he does not look to the future or think about the past. But the wise man both remembers the past and considers the future. So every wise mind walks backward, that is, looks at the past, and is not hindered by any habit of nature. It allows nothing of its deeds to be empty, nothing to be naked. Whatever was done amiss it covers with a sort of garment and with the grace of present or future work, so that it passes over nothing unseemly and leaves nothing unadorned. Hence the apostle too forgot what lay behind and reached out for what lay ahead. But he forgot in order to hide the errors of his persecution, to cover his former offences and overshadow them with good works. For blessed also are those whose sins are covered, that is, if they are covered by good deeds and veiled by the disciplines of virtue that follow.

"And Noah," it says, "became sober from the wine." It is clear that men become sober from drunkenness after sleep has intervened, but the mind is sober when it knows both the past and the future. So the mind of the righteous man was sober even when it was thought drunk, for glorious is the cup that inebriates the righteous. But the one who laughed at his father was truly drunk. Since he considered neither the past grace of his begetting, nor the reverence due his father in the present, nor the future punishment for wronging a father, he was truly drunk and did not see what he thought he saw. There was deep blindness in one who could not see his father. For had he seen his father, he certainly would not have laughed; a father is not to be laughed at but revered. Much less could the fool see the mind of the righteous man. For how could he see, who thought there was the error of drunkenness where there was the perfect vapour of wisdom and the other virtues? As it is written: "For she is the vapour of the power of God." When is the mind more sober than when it so contemplates the nature of all things and the affairs of present and future times that no temporal staggering of drunkenness appears in it?

I also ask why, when he earlier made Ham the middle one among the sons, he now makes him the younger. For it is written: "Noah knew all that his younger son had done to him." Did Scripture err earlier in the order of birth? Certainly not. What then? Is what is now written contradictory? I do not think so. How then is it resolved, unless you take "younger" not in age or time, but as meaning raw in understanding and still in a kind of infancy of intellect, one who has not drunk in the teaching of a riper age or taken in the counsel of the old? For men's understanding is a kind of grey hair. And so it says: "When you come to the council of the elders, shut your mouth," as a saying puts it elsewhere; for you must learn before you speak. So keep your ears ready, so that you may gain something from the counsels of the wise. The tongue must be restrained, the hearing made ready.

Blessing his son Shem, Noah said: "Blessed be the Lord God of Shem, and Canaan shall be his servant." He said both "Lord" and "God," and specifically the God of his son named Shem, because he is the God of the righteous, that is, the God of minds, not of valleys, of minds that possess the grace of lofty virtue. Next, why, when it was his son Ham who sinned, did he consign not Ham himself but Ham's son to slavery? Perhaps because a father is more affected by wrongs done to his son, especially those of which he himself is guilty and the cause, and is more deeply grieved that the condemnation for his own sin is paid by his son, who is punished not so much for his own deserts as for his father's. Then again, since the son was the pupil of his father's teaching and imitated his worst thoughts, the two had as it were one body and one mind and the same malice. So it makes no difference whether the son paid the price for his father's malice or for his own, since wickedness is a shared partnership. Whatever he paid for his father's wickedness, then, he doubtless paid for his own as well, being guilty of the same fault. Or at any rate the punishment is prolonged when it extends even to the son, and the affliction of the successor is drawn out over

many ages. So much for the letter. For the rest, it is not so much men who are meant here as characters, which in both have one nature. For Ham means "heat," Canaan "commotion" and "restlessness." Whoever is hot is surely restless and more agitated. So in the two there was one passion and one disposition.

Therefore when one is consigned, both are condemned. Why then did holy Noah, blessing his son Japheth, say: "May the Lord enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the houses of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant"? We said above that Japheth signifies, as it were, the indifferent good. What is indifferent has breadth, which lies in health, vigour, beauty, strength, wealth, favour, noble birth, friends, powers and the like. But though these indifferent things are goods, they have harmed many who did not possess them with wisdom and justice. For riches have made many drunk, noble birth and power have made them proud, beauty has made them dissolute, and with its help they have corrupted the chastity of another's mind. So these things we have mentioned are indifferent according to the disposition of the one who uses them: either their use is governed by the virtues, or, without the guidance of the virtues, things that could be useful begin to do harm.

Now we think we must by no means pass over the fact that Noah is said to have lived three hundred and fifty years after the flood. For it is certain that the three hundred signify the cross of Christ, by whose type the righteous man was delivered from the flood. In the fifty is the jubilee, the number of remission, on which the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven, pouring grace into human hearts. So the righteous man completed the course of this life with the perfect number of remission and grace.

Of the descendants of Japheth it says: "Rhodes and the other islands of the nations." Not without reason is he called "breadth," since his descendants advanced even into the other part of nature, that is, the sea. Truly, being breadth, it was not content with what nature had appointed for human use, namely the possession of the land, but even entered the sea and advanced as far as the islands. So much for the letter.

According to the higher sense, it is because external things, which are called goods—riches, powers, honours—spread themselves more widely, as it were. The rich are not content with what is in their hands and before their eyes, but spread their desires far and wide, seeking money and gain from more distant places, or honour from more people, or more far-reaching power, or the satisfaction of their desire.

Now I ask why Scripture recorded that Cush, the son of that wicked Ham, was the elder. There are two kinds of earth: one sandy and dusty—or, to put it more plainly, dust—and another kind fruitful and fertile, that is, more solid and deep earth. What then does the wicked man beget but dust, from which no offspring can come? And so the prophet compared the impious to dust, saying: "Not so the impious, not so, but like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth." For according to the higher sense too, the soul of the impious is barren and cannot produce useful fruit.

And why does Cush beget Nimrod the giant, who was a hunter before God? This is why it was said: "Like Nimrod, the giant hunter before God." What else, then, would dust and sand beget but an earthly man, since the ungodly man puts earthly things before heavenly ones? For legend tells that the giants wanted to fight against the powers above, and thought they could climb up to heaven by an earthly ascent.

In a deeper sense, however, this signifies that whoever loves earthly pleasures and follows them, and thinks that through them he can reach the grace of God, and that the kingdom of heaven is to be granted to errors of this kind, is waging war against heavenly things with a defiant spirit. That is why the proverb says of someone who has done wrong: "Like Nimrod, the giant hunter before God." Now the name Nimrod is interpreted as "Ethiopian." The Ethiopian's color signifies the darkness and squalor of a soul that is hostile to the light, without any share in brightness, wrapped in darkness, more like night than day. A hunter, too, spends his life in the vast forests among wild animals and beasts. So, being irrational himself, he mingles with irrational passions, and a hunter of this kind habitually searches out whatever belongs to a wild and harsh wickedness, and takes possession of it and delights in it. Finally, the beginning of this Nimrod's kingdom is Babylon, that is, "confusion," because wickedness and power are found not in simplicity and purity, nor in the clear order of virtue, but in the confusion of vices.
